metadata.remarks:
Content licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. The AACF name and logo are not covered by that licence.

Each control is scored from 0 to 5; Level 3 is the baseline:

- Level 0 Absent: Confirmed absent: the evidence shows nothing is in place. Not known is recorded as insufficient evidence, not 0.
- Level 1 Initial: Happens through individual effort; undocumented and inconsistent.
- Level 2 Developing: Some practice and documentation, but partial, local or not yet enforced.
- Level 3 Defined: Documented, owned, resourced and applied across the organisation.
- Level 4 Managed: Measured, assured and reported; exceptions are caught and acted on.
- Level 5 Optimising: Improved continuously against measured outcomes and external change.

Properties in the namespace https://aacf.adriansaxton.com/ns/oscal are AACF terms: applies (the overlay a criterion depends on: core, PUB, PRV, HIR, GEN, AGT or BLD), accountable-role and contributing-role, lifecycle-stage, and cross-reference, whose value is a source code and a clause, item or risk identifier, with class direct (met at Level 3) or partial. Cross-references are the author's interpretation and are not a compliance finding. Source codes are listed in back-matter.

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Sets out what the organisation wants from AI and how that serves its wider strategy: the ambition, the boundaries, the funding, the expected value and the roadmap. The aim is adoption driven by the organisation's own objectives, with choices made deliberately and revisited as technology, rules and expectations change.

controls.title: AI ambition aligned to organisational strategy

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has a stated ambition for AI that is derived from its own strategy and objectives, and that leaders and staff can describe. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved AI ambition states what AI is for in terms of the organisation's objectives.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI ambition has a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI ambition has been communicated across the organisation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI adopted for its own sake produces scattered pilots that do not add up to anything the organisation needs. Tying the ambition to existing objectives gives every later decision on funding, priority and risk a test to apply: does this help us do what we are here to do.

Reaching Level 3:

- List the organisation's current strategic objectives and, for each one, write down where AI could help and where it has no part to play.
- Draft a short ambition of one page that says what AI is for in terms of those objectives, not in terms of technology.
- Name a senior owner for the ambition and get it approved by leadership through the normal decision route.
- Communicate the approved ambition to all staff through existing channels and include it in AI induction material (see CUL-02 and PPL-01).

Pitfalls:

- Writing a vision about the technology that could belong to any organisation and gives no test for choosing between proposals.
- Getting approval but never telling staff, so the ambition exists only in a board paper.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What is the organisation trying to achieve with AI, and which organisational objectives does that serve?
- Who approved the ambition, and where is it written down?
- Can you show a recent AI decision that was tested against the ambition?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved AI ambition or strategy, showing links to organisational objectives
- Approval record from the board or executive committee
- Decision papers that refer to the ambition

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No stated ambition; AI activity is driven by individual interest or supplier offers.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: An ambition or vision statement exists, but it is generic, not linked to organisational objectives, or not agreed by leadership.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An approved AI ambition, owned by a named person and expressed in terms of the organisation's objectives, is known across the organisation.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progress against the ambition is measured and reported, and AI activity that does not serve it is identified and challenged.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The ambition is refined from evidence of what AI has delivered and from changes in the organisation's strategy.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- One-page AI ambition statement linked to organisational objectives
- Objective to AI opportunity mapping table
- Staff briefing note on the AI ambition

controls.title: Where AI will and will not be used

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has decided, and recorded with reasons, the areas of its work where AI is encouraged, where it is allowed only under conditions, and where it is ruled out. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Approved strategic boundaries set out the areas where AI is encouraged, allowed only under conditions, or ruled out, with the reason for each.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The strategic boundaries are consistent with the approved AI risk appetite (RSK-01).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI policy (GOV-01) reflects the strategic boundaries.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The strategic boundaries name the kinds of decision that must always be taken by a person.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Staff and suppliers need to know where effort is welcome and where it is not, before they invest time in a proposal. Stating the reasons lets people apply the boundaries to cases the list does not name, and lets the organisation revisit them when the reasons change.

Reaching Level 3:

- Work through the organisation's main areas of work and sort each into encouraged, conditional or ruled out for AI, writing the reason for each choice.
- Check each boundary against the approved risk appetite (RSK-01) and adjust any that would accept more risk than it allows.
- List the kinds of decision that must always be taken by a person, such as those with serious effects on someone's rights or livelihood.
- Get the boundaries approved and make sure the AI policy (GOV-01) reflects them, including the decisions reserved for people.

Pitfalls:

- Recording the categories without the reasons, so nobody can apply them to a new case.
- Setting boundaries that contradict the risk appetite or the policy, leaving staff unsure which applies.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which areas of your work are you actively seeking to use AI in, and which have you ruled out?
- What reasons are recorded for the areas that are ruled out or conditional?
- How do the boundaries show up in the AI policy and in how proposals are judged?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved statement of strategic boundaries, with reasons
- Cross-references between the boundaries, the risk appetite and the AI policy

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No stated boundaries; whether AI is suitable for an area is argued case by case, if at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some areas are informally favoured or avoided, but this is not written down, not reasoned, or not agreed by leadership.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Approved strategic boundaries say where AI is encouraged, conditional or ruled out and why, fit the risk appetite and the policy, and keep some decisions with people.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Proposals and live uses are checked against the boundaries, and pressure on them (repeated requests in a ruled-out area, for example) is reported and considered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Boundaries are adjusted from evidence such as outcomes, incidents and external change, and the reasons for each change are published internally.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI boundaries table with encouraged, conditional and ruled-out areas and reasons
- List of decisions reserved for people

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has a defined approach to funding AI, covering what is paid for centrally and locally, how long commitments last, and how requests for money are judged. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented funding approach sets out which AI costs are the responsibility of central budgets and which of local budgets.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The funding approach provides multi-year commitments where the work needs them.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Criteria for judging requests for AI funding are published.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Funding decisions across the organisation follow the documented approach.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI needs some shared spending (platforms, skills, governance) that no single team will fund, and much of its value only appears after more than one budget year. Without a funding approach, promising work stops when a pilot budget runs out, and money goes to whoever asks first rather than to what serves the ambition.

Reaching Level 3:

- Decide which AI costs are paid centrally (for example shared platforms, licences and governance) and which are paid by individual teams.
- Identify which AI commitments need funding over more than one year, such as platforms, contracts and skills, and agree how they are protected.
- Write and publish the criteria used to judge funding requests, linked to the value case (STR-04) and prioritisation criteria (POR-02).
- Document the funding approach, get it approved by finance and leadership, and apply it to every AI funding request from then on.

Pitfalls:

- Funding AI only through one-year pilot budgets, so successful uses have no money to run once the pilot ends.
- Publishing criteria but letting requests bypass them through local budgets.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How is AI work funded, and what is paid for centrally versus by individual teams?
- Can work that proves itself in a pilot get funding to run and scale beyond the current year?
- How are competing requests for AI funding judged, and by whom?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The documented funding approach or investment framework for AI
- Budget papers showing AI allocations, including any multi-year commitments
- Records of recent funding decisions against the stated criteria

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI is funded from whatever local budgets teams can find; there is no view of total spend.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some central or ring-fenced funding exists, but the rules for accessing it are unclear, it is year to year only, or it covers pilots and not running costs.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A documented approach to funding AI sets central and local responsibilities, longer commitments where needed and published criteria, and is followed across the organisation.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Total AI spend is known and reported against the funding approach, and funded work is reviewed against what it was funded to deliver.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Funding allocation is adjusted from evidence of which investments delivered value, and the approach is refined each planning cycle.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI funding approach note setting out central and local responsibilities
- Published funding request criteria and scoring sheet

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has stated the value it expects from AI across its work, by type of value, with the assumptions behind each estimate written down. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved value case sets out the efficiency, quality, service and capability gains expected from AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The value case states the assumptions behind the expected gains.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The value case has a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Strategy and funding decisions refer to the value case.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
An organisation-level value case lets leaders judge whether the overall investment is worth making and which kinds of value to pursue first. Writing the assumptions down means they can be tested later, so the case improves rather than becoming a figure nobody can check.

Reaching Level 3:

- Estimate the value expected from AI under four headings: efficiency, quality, service and capability.
- Write down the assumptions behind each estimate, including what the comparison is and how confident the estimate is.
- Name an owner for the value case and get it approved alongside the AI ambition (STR-01).
- Use the value case when making strategy and funding decisions (STR-03), and set up tracking of whether benefits arrive through MON-03.

Pitfalls:

- Counting only time saved and ignoring quality, service and capability gains.
- Leaving assumptions unstated, so estimates cannot be challenged or checked later.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What value does the organisation expect from AI overall, and of what kinds?
- What assumptions sit behind those estimates, and who owns them?
- When did you last check the value case against what live uses have actually delivered?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The organisation-level value case, with assumptions recorded
- Strategy or funding papers that draw on it
- A comparison of the value case with tracked benefits

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No organisation-level view of expected value; benefits are claimed use by use, if at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Expected value is described in general terms, without estimates, assumptions or a split by type of value.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An approved, owned value case states the gains expected from AI and the assumptions behind them, and is used in strategy and funding decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The value case is compared with tracked benefits from live uses, and assumptions that prove wrong are reported and corrected.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The value case is refined each cycle from measured outcomes, and its accuracy over time is itself tracked.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Organisation-level AI value case with assumptions log
- Value type definitions for efficiency, quality, service and capability

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation tracks changes in AI technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation, and feeds what it finds into its AI strategy. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined horizon scanning activity covers AI technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The scanning activity has a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The scanning activity produces output on a regular cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Scanning findings are considered in strategy decisions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI capability, rules and public attitudes are changing faster than most planning cycles. An organisation that does not look outward will find its strategy overtaken, or will learn of a new obligation or a better approach from someone else.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name an owner for horizon scanning and agree the four areas it covers: technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation.
- Choose a small set of sources for each area and set a regular cycle, such as quarterly, for reviewing them.
- Produce a short regular summary of what has changed and what it could mean for the organisation.
- Put each summary on the agenda of the forum or person that makes AI strategy decisions and record what was decided (see STR-08).

Pitfalls:

- Collecting news without saying what it means for the organisation.
- Scanning only technology and missing changes in regulation or public expectation.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How does the organisation keep track of changes in AI technology, regulation and practice elsewhere?
- Who receives the findings, and can you show a strategy decision that one of them changed?
- How do you find out how the people you serve feel about AI being used?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Horizon scanning outputs, such as briefings or a log of developments
- Records showing findings were considered by the forum or in strategy papers

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No organised scanning; individuals follow developments informally and share them ad hoc.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some scanning happens, for example a newsletter or occasional briefing, but it is not linked to strategy decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An owned horizon scanning activity covers technology, regulation, peers and public expectation, produces regular output and informs strategy decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Findings are logged with the action taken on each, and the time from a relevant external change to a strategy response is tracked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Scanning anticipates change well enough that the organisation acts ahead of it, and the scanning sources and method are reviewed against how useful they proved.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Horizon scanning source list by area
- Quarterly horizon scan summary template

controls.title: Multi-year AI roadmap tied to planning

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has a phased AI roadmap that is linked to its business and financial planning cycles and shows the points where it will decide whether to proceed. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved, phased AI roadmap covers several years.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The roadmap is aligned with the organisation's business and financial planning cycles.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The roadmap names its decision points and the criteria for each.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The roadmap has a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The roadmap names the capability, data and technology capacity, including compute and storage, that planned uses depend on, and shows which uses depend on which.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A strategy without a roadmap is hard to fund and hard to hold anyone to. Linking the roadmap to normal planning cycles means AI work competes for resources in the same process as everything else, and explicit decision points stop the organisation drifting into large commitments without choosing to.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set out the planned AI work in phases over several years, aligned to the organisation's business and financial planning cycles.
- Name the decision points in the roadmap and the criteria for deciding whether to proceed, change course or stop at each.
- For each phase, list the capability, data and technology capacity (including compute and storage) that the planned uses depend on, and the dependencies between them.
- Name an owner for the roadmap and get it approved through the same route as business plans and budgets.

Pitfalls:

- Producing a list of projects with dates but no decision points, so the roadmap is never questioned.
- Planning uses without the data, skills and compute they depend on.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there a roadmap for AI, and how far ahead does it look?
- How does it connect to the organisation's business plan and budget cycle?
- What are the next decision points, and what will each decision be based on?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved roadmap, with phases and decision points
- Business or financial planning documents that reference it
- Records of decisions taken at roadmap decision points
- Roadmap entries for enabling capability, data and compute capacity, with dependencies

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No roadmap; AI work is planned project by project, if at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A roadmap exists but is a list of projects, is not linked to business or financial planning, or has no decision points.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An approved, owned multi-year roadmap follows the planning cycles, sets decision points with criteria and names the capacity planned uses depend on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progress against the roadmap is reported, decisions at each point are recorded with their evidence, and slippage is acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The roadmap is revised each planning cycle from delivery evidence, value achieved and external change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Phased AI roadmap with decision points and criteria
- Dependency register for capability, data and technology capacity

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Staff, their representatives, service users, partners and, where relevant, the public and regulators have a real opportunity to shape the AI strategy, and the organisation can show what changed as a result. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A planned engagement approach identifies the stakeholder groups relevant to the AI strategy.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The identified groups are involved before the strategy is settled.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A record shows the input from each group and the organisation's response to it.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
The people who do the work and the people affected by it see risks and opportunities that leaders do not. Involving them early produces a better strategy and makes it more likely to be accepted, while consultation after decisions are made does neither.

Reaching Level 3:

- Identify the stakeholder groups that should shape the AI strategy, such as staff, their representatives, service users, partners and, where relevant, the public and regulators.
- Plan how and when each group will be involved, making sure it happens before the strategy is settled.
- Run the engagement and record what each group said.
- Record how the strategy responded to each main point, including where input was not taken up and why, and share that response with the groups (see CUL-03).

Pitfalls:

- Consulting on a strategy that is already decided, so input cannot change anything.
- Recording what people said but not what was done about it.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Who was involved in shaping the AI strategy, and at what stage?
- Which groups affected by your use of AI have not been heard?
- Can you point to something in the strategy that changed because of stakeholder input?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The stakeholder engagement plan for the strategy
- A record of input received and how the strategy responded

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: The strategy is written by a small group without wider input.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some groups are consulted, but late, selectively, or with no record of what they said or what changed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A planned engagement approach involves the relevant stakeholder groups before the strategy is settled and records what they said and how the organisation responded.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The reach and influence of engagement are measured, gaps in who has been heard are identified, and stakeholders are told what changed because of them.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Stakeholder involvement is a continuing part of how the strategy is developed, and the approach is improved from participants' feedback.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Stakeholder engagement plan for the AI strategy
- Input and response log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The AI strategy is reviewed on a set cycle and whenever defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI strategy has a set review cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Defined triggers, such as major regulatory, technology or organisational change, prompt a review outside the cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each review is carried out by the strategy's owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Changes to the strategy are recorded with their reasons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A strategy written for one state of the technology and the rules will be wrong within a year or two. A fixed cycle keeps it current, defined triggers catch changes that cannot wait, and a change record lets people see why direction shifted.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set a review cycle for the AI strategy, such as yearly, aligned to business planning.
- Define the triggers that require a review outside the cycle, such as major regulatory, technology or organisational change, and link them to horizon scanning (STR-05).
- Make the strategy owner responsible for carrying out each review and reporting the result to leadership.
- Keep a change log that records each change to the strategy with its reason and date.

Pitfalls:

- Setting triggers that nobody watches for, so only the yearly review ever happens.
- Changing the strategy without recording why, so later readers cannot follow its history.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- When was the AI strategy last reviewed, and when is the next review due?
- What events would cause an unscheduled review?
- What changed at the last review, and why?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Strategy version history or change log, with reasons
- Papers and minutes from the most recent review

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: The strategy is not reviewed once written, or is rewritten only when leadership changes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Reviews happen, but irregularly, without defined triggers, or without a record of what changed and why.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: The AI strategy is reviewed by its owner on a set cycle and when defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Reviews draw on measured evidence such as value achieved, risk and incident trends and horizon scanning, and actions from each review are tracked to completion.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The review cycle and triggers are themselves adjusted from experience, so the strategy is updated at the pace the organisation needs.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Strategy review schedule and trigger list
- Strategy change log

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Sets out who is accountable for AI, how decisions about AI are made and recorded, and how the organisation keeps sight of the AI it uses. Governance here should be proportionate: light enough that low-risk use is not slowed, firm enough that high-risk use cannot happen without the right people deciding.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has an approved AI policy that states which uses of AI are permitted, which need approval and which are not allowed, and keeps it current. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved AI policy states which parts of the organisation, uses and systems AI governance covers.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The policy states which uses of AI are permitted, which need approval and which are prohibited.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The policy's prohibited uses include the practices that the law bans.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The policy has a named owner and a review date.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The policy has been communicated to all staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The policy and its supporting governance documents are approved, version-controlled and retained.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Acceptable use terms are set for users of AI services the organisation offers to others, and are reviewed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Breaches of the acceptable use terms by users of the organisation's AI services are acted on.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without a policy, staff either avoid AI entirely or use it without guardrails. A clear policy is the first thing people look for and the basis every other control refers to.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a policy that states what AI governance covers (which parts of the organisation, which uses and which systems) and sorts uses into permitted, approval-required and prohibited, with practices banned by law listed as prohibited.
- Where the organisation offers AI services to others, set acceptable use terms for those users and decide how they are enforced and reviewed.
- Name a policy owner and review date, get the policy approved, and keep it and its supporting governance documents under version control and retention.
- Communicate the policy to all staff and check they know where to find it (see PPL-01 and GOV-08).

Pitfalls:

- Writing a policy that lists principles but never says which uses are allowed, need approval or are banned.
- Letting supporting documents drift out of version control so nobody knows which is current.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there an AI policy approved at the right level, and when was it last reviewed?
- Does it distinguish uses that are permitted, need approval, and are not allowed?
- How would a member of staff find it, and how do you know they have?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved policy, with owner, approval record and review date
- Communication or training records showing staff were told about it
- Change history showing reviews have happened
- A stated scope for AI governance, and version control and retention for governance documents
- Practices banned by law included in the prohibited list

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No organisation-wide policy; individual teams or staff set their own rules.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A policy or guidance note exists but is incomplete, unapproved, or not widely known.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An approved, owned and controlled AI policy sets the scope of AI governance and which uses are permitted, need approval or are prohibited, and all staff know it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Policy awareness and compliance are measured; the policy is reviewed on schedule and after significant incidents or external change.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The policy is refined from evidence of how AI is actually used, incidents and lessons, and stays ahead of external change rather than reacting to it.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI policy template with scope, permitted, approval-required and prohibited uses
- Acceptable use terms for external users of AI services
- Governance document register with versions and retention

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A named senior executive is accountable for the organisation's use of AI, with a defined remit, and reports on it to the board or equivalent. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A named senior executive is formally accountable for the organisation's use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A written remit sets out that executive's accountability for AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: AI is a standing item in the executive's reporting to the board or equivalent.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI cuts across technology, data, risk and the business. Without one accountable executive it falls between functions, decisions stall and nobody owns the outcome.

Reaching Level 3:

- Choose a senior executive to be accountable for the organisation's use of AI and confirm it formally through the usual appointment route.
- Write a short remit covering what they are accountable for, what they can decide and what they must escalate.
- Make AI a standing item in that executive's regular reporting to the board or equivalent, drawing on MON-08.

Pitfalls:

- Giving accountability to a technical lead without the seniority to stop or redirect AI work.
- Splitting accountability between several executives so nobody owns the whole picture.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Who is accountable for AI across the organisation, and where is that written down?
- What authority does that person have over budget, risk acceptance and stopping a use of AI?
- How often does the board or equivalent hear about AI, and what does it receive?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Terms of reference, role description or scheme of delegation naming the accountable executive
- Board or executive committee papers and minutes covering AI

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No one is accountable; AI is treated as a technology matter or left to enthusiasts.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Someone is informally seen as the lead, but the remit is unclear or lacks authority.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A named senior executive is formally accountable for AI under a written remit and reports on AI to the board or equivalent as a standing item.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The board receives regular, evidence-based reporting on AI benefits, risks and performance, and challenges it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Accountability arrangements are reviewed against outcomes and adjusted as AI use grows or changes in nature.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Accountable executive remit
- Board AI report template

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Decision rights for approving, changing and retiring uses of AI are defined, scaled to risk, and followed. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Defined decision rights, tiered by residual risk, state who can approve, change and retire each class of AI use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The decision rights are applied across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The approval route screens each proposed use of AI against prohibited practices.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A use whose residual risk cannot be brought within the risk appetite is not approved, or is stopped.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
If every use needs the same approval, low-risk use is choked and people work around the process. If none does, high-risk use goes ahead unseen. Tiered decision rights give speed where it is safe and scrutiny where it matters.

Reaching Level 3:

- Group uses of AI into risk tiers based on residual risk from the risk assessment (RSK-02).
- For each tier, write down who can approve, change and retire a use, and publish this as a decision rights table.
- Add a screening step at the start of the approval route that checks each proposal against prohibited practices in the policy (GOV-01).
- Make it a rule that a use whose residual risk cannot be brought within the risk appetite (RSK-01) is refused or stopped, and record such decisions.
- Apply the decision rights to every AI use across the organisation and check a sample each year for compliance (see GOV-08).

Pitfalls:

- Covering approval but not change or retirement, so material changes slip through unreviewed.
- Sending every use to the same senior forum, which creates a queue and encourages workarounds.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Who can approve a new use of AI, and does that depend on its risk?
- Who can change or switch off a use of AI once it is live?
- How would you know if a use of AI went live without approval?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Documented decision rights or approval matrix by risk tier
- A sample of approval records for recent uses of AI

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No defined approval route; uses of AI start wherever someone decides to try them.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: An approval route exists for some uses or some parts of the organisation, or is the same for all uses regardless of risk.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Risk-tiered decision rights for approving, changing and retiring uses of AI are applied everywhere, screen out prohibited practices and stop uses beyond the risk appetite.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Decisions are recorded and periodically checked against the tiers; bypasses are detected and dealt with.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Tiers and thresholds are adjusted from evidence such as time to decision, incidents and outcomes, so the route stays proportionate.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Decision rights table by risk tier for approve, change and retire
- Prohibited practice screening checklist

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A cross-functional forum oversees AI use, risk and performance, with terms of reference, the right membership and a clear link to the organisation's main governance. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An AI oversight forum has terms of reference.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The forum's membership is cross-functional and brings diverse demographic backgrounds and lived experience.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The forum has a defined escalation route.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The forum meets on a set cycle and records its decisions.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI decisions need technology, data, legal, security, people and business views in the same room. A standing forum gives that, and gives the accountable executive somewhere to take decisions that are bigger than one team.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write terms of reference for an AI oversight forum covering purpose, remit, decision powers, quorum and how it reports to the main governance.
- Appoint cross-functional members (for example business, data, technology, risk, legal and people), and seek members with diverse demographic backgrounds and lived experience, including from outside the usual senior group if needed.
- Define an escalation route from the forum to the board or equivalent, and from delivery teams to the forum.
- Set a meeting cycle and keep minutes that record decisions and actions.

Pitfalls:

- Filling the forum with technical staff only, so ethical and service effects are missed.
- Treating diversity as a box ticked by job title rather than by background and experience.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there a group that oversees AI, and what can it decide on its own?
- Which functions sit on it, and who is missing?
- Where do its decisions go, and how do you know they are acted on?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Terms of reference and membership list
- Agendas, minutes and a decision or action log

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No forum; AI matters surface ad hoc in other meetings, if at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: An informal group or community of interest meets, but it has no remit to decide or escalate.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A diverse, cross-functional oversight forum works to terms of reference, meets on a set cycle, records its decisions and can escalate.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The forum tracks its decisions to completion and reports measured performance, risk and benefit to the accountable executive.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The forum's remit, membership and cadence are reviewed against its effect and adjusted as AI use matures.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI oversight forum terms of reference
- Membership matrix covering functions and backgrounds
- Decision and action log template

controls.title: Named owners for each use of AI

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every use of AI has named owners for the business outcome, the data, the technology and its assurance, recorded where others can find them. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every use of AI has named business, data, technical and assurance owners recorded in the AI inventory (GOV-06).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Ownership of a use of AI is handed over through a formal, recorded step.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The receiving owner records acceptance of the use's residual risk.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
When something goes wrong, or a decision is needed, the question is always who owns this. Named owners per use turn organisation-wide accountability into something that works in practice.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define the four owner roles for each use of AI: business, data, technical and assurance, with a short description of each.
- Name an owner for each role for every use and record them in the AI inventory (GOV-06).
- Set a handover process for when an owner changes, in which the receiving owner reviews and records acceptance of the residual risk.

Pitfalls:

- Naming a team or mailbox as owner instead of a person.
- Letting ownership lapse when people move roles, leaving uses with no owner.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a given use of AI, who owns the business outcome, the data and the technology?
- What happens to ownership when one of those people leaves or moves role?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Ownership fields in the AI inventory
- Evidence that ownership is updated on staff changes
- Ownership handover records with residual risk acceptance

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Ownership is assumed rather than assigned; often only the person who set it up knows.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some uses have a named owner, usually technical, but business and data ownership are gaps.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every use of AI has named business, data, technical and assurance owners in the inventory, and ownership changes hands formally with residual risk accepted.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Ownership is checked when people move roles, and gaps are caught and filled within a set time.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Owners actively manage their uses against measures, and ownership arrangements are improved from experience.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Owner role descriptions for business, data, technical and assurance owners
- Ownership handover form with residual risk acceptance

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation keeps a current inventory of the AI it uses, including AI built into bought products and services, with enough detail to govern it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A maintained AI inventory covers in-house, procured and embedded AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each inventory entry records its purpose, owners, risk tier and status.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each inventory entry records its regulatory risk classification and the reasons for it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each inventory entry records the supplier or source of the use and of its components.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each inventory entry is linked to its models, data sets and integrations.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each agent, the inventory records the tools, systems and data it can act on, and what it can do without a person's approval.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
An organisation cannot govern, secure or explain AI it does not know it has. A growing share of AI arrives inside products already in use, so an inventory of in-house builds alone gives a false sense of control.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set up an inventory with fields for purpose, owners, risk tier, regulatory risk classification with reasons, status, and the supplier or source of the use and its components.
- Find AI in use by asking teams, checking procurement and licence records, and reviewing products with built-in AI features, covering in-house, procured and embedded AI.
- Link each entry to its models, data sets and integrations, using existing data and system catalogues where they exist (see DAT-04 and TEC-04).
- Name an inventory owner and make updating it part of go-live, change and retirement (POR-03 and POR-09).

Pitfalls:

- Missing AI built into everyday products such as office suites and service platforms.
- Building the inventory once and never updating it.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there a list of the AI in use, and who keeps it up to date?
- Does it include AI built into products and services you have bought?
- How would a new use of AI get onto it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- For each agent: the tools, systems and data it can act on, and its approval thresholds
- The inventory itself, with a recent update date
- The process or form that adds and removes entries
- Regulatory classification and reasons recorded against inventory entries

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No inventory; knowledge of what AI is in use is scattered or absent.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A partial list exists, usually of in-house projects, missing AI embedded in bought products or used informally.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A maintained inventory covers in-house, procured and embedded AI, with the details needed to govern each entry and links to its models, data and integrations.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The inventory is reconciled against procurement, technology and data records, and its completeness is measured.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The inventory feeds portfolio, risk and transparency reporting automatically and is used as the organisation's single view of AI.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI inventory template with required fields
- Discovery questionnaire for teams and suppliers

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI governance works through the organisation's existing risk, information, data protection, security and procurement governance rather than alongside it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Risk, information management, data protection, security, procurement, safety and quality management, internal audit and business continuity processes each have a defined AI step.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI governance route calls on those processes rather than repeating them.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Uses of AI that could contribute to physical harm have a hazard analysis that feeds the relevant safety case.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Information governance and data protection advice is brought in at the start of design for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Information governance and data protection advisers have authority to require changes to a use of AI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A separate AI governance track duplicates effort, confuses people and leaves gaps where the two meet. Most AI questions are existing questions with a new twist, and the existing owners should answer them.

Reaching Level 3:

- List the existing governance processes (risk, information management, data protection, security, procurement, safety and quality management, internal audit and business continuity) and add a defined AI step to each.
- For uses that could contribute to physical harm, require a hazard analysis and feed its results into the relevant safety case.
- Design the AI approval route so it calls on these processes for their parts rather than repeating their checks.
- Bring information governance and data protection advisers in at the start of design, and give them authority to require changes.

Pitfalls:

- Building a separate AI process that duplicates existing checks and frustrates delivery teams.
- Involving data protection advisers only at the end, when changes are expensive.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- When a use of AI is proposed, which existing governance processes does it go through?
- Where do AI decisions duplicate or bypass existing processes?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Process maps or guidance showing the AI steps in existing governance
- Examples of AI cases handled through those routes
- The AI step in safety and quality management, and hazard analyses for uses that could cause physical harm

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI is handled entirely outside existing governance, or ignored by it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some links exist, for example data protection reviews AI cases, but the routes are informal and inconsistent.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Existing governance processes each have a defined AI step that the AI route calls on, with information and data protection advice involved from the start.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Hand-offs between AI and existing governance are tracked, and duplication or gaps are identified and closed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: AI considerations are part of how existing governance normally works, and no separate track is needed for routine decisions.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Governance integration map showing the AI step in each process
- Hazard analysis template for AI uses

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Compliance with the AI policy is monitored, and exceptions are requested, approved, recorded and reviewed. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Compliance with the AI policy is checked on a defined basis.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A recorded exception process, with approval and expiry dates, is in use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each exception record states the exception's risk and its treatment.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A policy nobody checks is advice. Recorded exceptions also show where the policy is out of step with real need, which is the best input to its next revision.

Reaching Level 3:

- Decide how compliance with the AI policy will be checked, such as an annual sample of uses and a self-declaration by owners, and how often.
- Set up an exception process in which each request records the risk, the treatment, the approver and an expiry date.
- Keep an exception register and review exceptions before they expire, either closing, renewing or escalating them.
- Report compliance findings and open exceptions to the oversight forum (GOV-04).

Pitfalls:

- Granting exceptions with no expiry, so they become permanent policy by the back door.
- Checking compliance only when something goes wrong.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you know whether the AI policy is being followed?
- If someone needs to do something the policy does not allow, what happens?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Compliance check records or reports
- The exceptions register, with approvals and expiry dates

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Compliance is not checked; exceptions happen informally or unseen.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Compliance is checked occasionally or after problems; exceptions are agreed verbally or by email without a record.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Compliance with the AI policy is checked on a defined basis, and exceptions go through a recorded process with approval, expiry, risk and treatment.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Compliance results and exception trends are reported to the oversight forum, and repeat exceptions trigger policy review.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Monitoring is largely built into tools and processes, and exception data routinely improves the policy.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Policy compliance check plan
- Exception request form and register

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation publishes information about how and why it uses AI, to the extent its obligations and public role require, and keeps it current. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each AI inventory entry, a recorded decision states whether a transparency record must be published, judged against the criteria that apply, and why.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Transparency records are published in the required format for all in-scope uses of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each published transparency record has a named owner and a review cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Transparency records are updated when a use changes materially or is retired.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each transparency record is checked through information access and security routes before release, with the reason recorded for anything withheld.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Any registration the law requires for a use of AI is completed before the use starts.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each use of AI, a recorded decision states whether its impact assessments are published, and why.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: External communications about sensitive uses of AI are cleared through a designated route.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Public bodies are expected to explain how they use algorithmic tools, and some are required to. Openness also builds trust and catches problems early, because people outside the organisation can see and question what it does.

Reaching Level 3:

- Find out which transparency obligations and formats apply, and for each inventory entry decide against those criteria whether a record must be published, recording the reason.
- Complete any registration the law requires before the use starts, and give each published record an owner and review cycle.
- Check each record through information access and security routes before release, recording the reason for anything withheld, and update records when a use changes materially or is retired.
- For each use, decide whether its impact assessments are published and record the reason.
- Set up a designated clearance route for external communications about sensitive uses of AI.

Pitfalls:

- Publishing records once and leaving them out of date as uses change.
- Withholding information without recording why, which cannot be defended if challenged.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which of your uses of AI are you required, or choose, to publish information about?
- Is what is published complete and current against the AI inventory?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Published transparency records or statements
- Reconciliation of published records against the inventory
- Registration records where the law requires them
- Publication decisions with reasons, update records, and pre-release checks showing reasons for anything withheld

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No public information about AI use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some information is published, for example a statement or a single record, but it is incomplete or out of date.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Decisions on what to publish about each use of AI are recorded, required records and registrations are completed and kept current, and sensitive communications are cleared.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Publication is checked against the AI inventory for completeness, and public questions and feedback are tracked and answered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Transparency is used as a design input: uses of AI are shaped so they can be explained publicly from the start.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Publication decision log per inventory entry
- Transparency record template in the required format
- Pre-release check and clearance procedure

controls.title: Review and disclosure of AI-generated content

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has approved rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content that it releases or relies on, so people know when AI was used. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Approved rules set how AI-generated content released outside the organisation, including synthetic media, is reviewed and disclosed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Approved rules set how AI-generated content used inside the organisation to inform decisions or form official records is reviewed and disclosed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The rules require disclosure at least to the extent the law requires, made clearly when a person first meets the content.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Review before release checks that AI-generated content does not reproduce others' protected work or copy a person's likeness or voice without permission.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Content produced by AI can be wrong or misleading, and can be mistaken for the work of a person. Reviewing it before it is released or relied on, and saying plainly where AI was used, protects the people who meet it and keeps official records trustworthy.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content released outside the organisation, including synthetic media such as images, audio and video.
- Extend the rules to AI-generated content used inside the organisation to inform decisions or form official records.
- Check the rules against the disclosure duties in the obligations register (RSK-04), and make disclosure clear at the point a person first meets the content.
- Approve the rules under the AI policy (GOV-01) and tell the staff who produce or publish content.

Pitfalls:

- Forgetting AI-generated content used internally, such as drafts that become official records.
- Placing the disclosure where people only find it after they have read or relied on the content.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Are there approved rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content released outside the organisation, including synthetic media?
- Do the rules also cover AI-generated content used inside the organisation to inform decisions or form official records?
- How and when is disclosure made, and how do you know it meets what the law requires?
- How does review check that released content does not reproduce protected work or copy someone's likeness or voice?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content, with owner and approval record
- A sample of released content and internal records showing review and disclosure
- The legal disclosure requirements the rules were checked against

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Whether AI-generated content is reviewed or disclosed is left to the person who produced it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some teams review or label AI-generated content, but the rules are incomplete, unapproved or not widely known, or content used inside the organisation is not covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Approved rules set how AI-generated content released outside the organisation, or used inside it for decisions and official records, is reviewed and disclosed, clearly and at least as the law requires.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Compliance with the review and disclosure rules is measured, and the rules are reviewed on schedule and after significant incidents or legal change.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The rules are refined from evidence of how AI-generated content is actually used and received, and stay ahead of external change rather than reacting to it.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI-generated content review and disclosure standard
- Disclosure wording for common content types

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Sets out how the organisation decides how much AI risk it will accept, assesses the risks and effects of each use of AI, and meets its legal, regulatory and ethical obligations. Assessment should be proportionate: a quick check for low-risk use, and deeper work where people's rights, safety or livelihoods could be affected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The board or equivalent has approved a statement of how much AI risk the organisation will accept, broken down by kind of risk, and it is used in decisions. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A board-approved AI risk appetite sets a tolerance for each relevant kind of risk, such as harm to people, legal, reputational and operational risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI risk appetite has a named owner and a review date.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Approval decisions on uses of AI refer to the risk appetite.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without a stated appetite, each approver applies their own tolerance, so similar uses get different answers and nobody can say whether the organisation is taking too much risk or too little. A board-approved appetite gives approvers a common reference and makes risk acceptance a deliberate choice.

Reaching Level 3:

- Agree the kinds of AI risk that matter to the organisation, for example harm to people, legal, reputational and operational.
- For each kind, write a tolerance statement saying what level of risk is acceptable, using the organisation's existing risk scale where possible.
- Name an owner and review date, and get the appetite approved by the board or equivalent.
- Add a reference to the appetite in AI approval templates so approvers must state how each decision fits it (see GOV-03).

Pitfalls:

- Writing one overall tolerance that does not separate different kinds of risk.
- Approving the appetite but never citing it in actual decisions.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Has the board approved a statement of how much AI risk the organisation will accept?
- Does it set different tolerances for different kinds of risk?
- How do approvers use it when deciding whether a use of AI can go ahead?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved AI risk appetite statement, with approval record and review date
- Approval records for uses of AI that refer to the appetite
- Risk reports comparing exposure with the appetite

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No statement of AI risk appetite; tolerance depends on whoever is deciding.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: AI is mentioned in the general risk appetite, or a draft AI statement exists, but it does not distinguish kinds of risk or is not approved.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A board-approved, owned AI risk appetite sets tolerances by kind of risk, has a review date and is referred to in approval decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Exposure across live and proposed uses is reported against the appetite, and decisions that exceed it are escalated and recorded.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The appetite is recalibrated from evidence of outcomes, incidents and external change, and the board reviews whether it is enabling the intended use of AI.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI risk appetite statement by kind of risk
- Approval template section referencing the appetite

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation uses one consistent, documented method to assess the risks of each use of AI, and the results feed its corporate risk management. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented AI risk assessment method, proportionate to risk tier, covers risks particular to AI as well as general risks.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every use of AI is assessed with the method before approval.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use of AI is assessed again during live use and on material change.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Assessment results are recorded in the corporate risk registers.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each assessment records the treatment chosen for each risk and the controls applied, with the reasons for choosing them.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each assessment records the residual risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The method covers the recognised generative AI risk categories.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Different teams assessing AI risk in different ways produce results that cannot be compared or added up. A single method, built into the existing risk process, lets the organisation see its overall AI risk and makes sure the risks particular to AI are not missed.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a risk assessment method with depth scaled to risk tier, covering AI-specific risks (such as error, drift, misuse and opacity) as well as general ones, and the recognised risk categories for generative AI.
- Require each assessment to record the treatment chosen for each risk, the controls applied with the reasons for choosing them, and the residual risk.
- Apply the method to every use before approval, and again during live use and on material change.
- Record results in the corporate risk registers using the organisation's standard scales.

Pitfalls:

- Assessing once at approval and never again as the use or its data changes.
- Keeping AI risks in a separate register that corporate risk management never sees.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How is the risk of a proposed use of AI assessed, and is the method the same across the organisation?
- Does the method cover risks particular to AI, such as wrong outputs, drift or misuse, alongside general ones?
- Where do assessment results go, and when is a use reassessed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The documented risk assessment method and guidance
- A sample of completed assessments for recent uses of AI
- Corporate or departmental risk registers showing AI risks
- Risk treatment records showing the controls selected for each use and why
- Reassessment records for live uses, with residual risk recorded

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI risk is assessed, if at all, by individual judgement with no common method.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A method or checklist exists, but it is used in some areas only, does not cover risks particular to AI, or sits outside corporate risk management.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A documented, proportionate method assesses every use of AI before approval and in live use, records treatment and residual risk, and feeds corporate risk registers.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Assessments are quality checked, and the AI risk profile, including trends in residual risk, is reported to the oversight forum.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The method is refined from incidents, near misses and assessment reviews, and its results are shown to predict where problems occur.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI risk assessment method and template by tier
- AI risk catalogue including generative AI categories
- Treatment and controls record with reasons

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before a use of AI goes live, its likely effects on people and groups (including equality, privacy, rights and safety) and on society and the environment are assessed to a depth that matches its risk, and the findings are acted on. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Impact assessments, proportionate to risk, cover equality, privacy (including sensitive inferences about people), rights and safety.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Impact assessments cover effects on the workforce: workload, working conditions, skills and progression.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Impact assessments cover wider societal and environmental effects.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An impact assessment is completed and signed off before each in-scope use of AI goes live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each impact assessment is kept current while the use is live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Mitigations identified in impact assessments are tracked.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For public-facing AI assistants, the impact assessment also covers over-reliance and people treating the AI as human.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Risk assessment looks at the risk to the organisation; impact assessment looks at what the use of AI could do to the people it touches. Some harms, such as a group being treated less favourably, only appear when someone asks that question directly and before the system is in use.

Reaching Level 3:

- Build an impact assessment template covering equality, privacy (including sensitive inferences about people), rights, safety, effects on the workforce (workload, working conditions, skills and progression) and wider societal and environmental effects.
- Add questions on over-reliance and people treating the AI as human for public-facing assistants.
- Scale the depth of assessment to risk and require sign-off before every in-scope use goes live.
- Track mitigations to completion and review the assessment during use and when the use changes.

Pitfalls:

- Treating the impact assessment as a form to finish rather than findings to act on.
- Leaving out effects on the organisation's own staff.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which uses of AI need an impact assessment before going live, and who decides?
- What does the assessment cover beyond data protection?
- Can you show a case where an impact assessment changed the design or stopped a deployment?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The impact assessment template and guidance on proportionality
- Completed and signed-off assessments for recent deployments
- Records of mitigations and their completion
- Impact assessment reviews during live use

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Effects on people are not assessed before go-live, or only after a complaint.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some impact assessment happens, for example for data protection, but equality, rights and safety are not covered consistently, or findings are not acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A proportionate impact assessment covering people, workforce, society and environment is signed off before each in-scope use goes live, kept current, and its mitigations tracked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Completion and quality of impact assessments are checked, assessments are revisited after significant change, and actual effects in live use are compared with what was predicted.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Impact assessment shapes design from the start, and the method is improved from evidence of effects it missed.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI impact assessment template with proportionate depth
- Mitigation tracker

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation keeps a current view of the laws, regulations and standards that apply to its use of AI, with an owner for each obligation and a way of checking it is met. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A maintained register lists the obligations that apply to the organisation's use of AI, with a named owner for each.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The register of obligations is reviewed on a set cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The register is used when uses of AI are designed and approved.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Legal advice is taken when each use of AI is designed and when it changes materially.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each use of AI, the organisation's regulatory role, for example provider or deployer, is recorded and checked again when the purpose, branding or system changes.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each use of AI, the reporting duties that follow from that role are recorded, with a named owner for contact with regulators.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each use of AI, a record shows how legal obligations are split between suppliers, the organisation and users.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each party is told its share of the legal obligations for a use of AI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Obligations on AI come from many places at once: data protection, equality, sector regulation, consumer and employment law, and new AI-specific rules. Without one maintained view, obligations are missed or each team interprets them differently.

Reaching Level 3:

- Build a register of laws, regulations and standards that apply to AI use, name an owner for each obligation and set a review cycle.
- For each use, record the organisation's regulatory role (for example provider or deployer), the reporting duties that follow and a named owner for contact with regulators, and re-check the role when purpose, branding or the system changes.
- Record for each use how legal obligations are split between suppliers, the organisation and users, and tell each party its share.
- Make the register part of design and approval, with legal advice taken at design and on material change.

Pitfalls:

- Treating the register as a legal team document that delivery teams never use.
- Missing a change of regulatory role when a bought system is rebranded or repurposed.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which laws, regulations and standards apply to your use of AI, and where is that recorded?
- Who owns each obligation, and how do you know it is being met?
- How would you find out about a new obligation, and how quickly would you act on it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The obligations register, with owners and review dates
- Compliance check records or legal sign-off for recent uses of AI
- Regulatory role recorded for each use, with re-check records and the named regulator contact

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No view of which obligations apply to AI use; legal advice is sought only when a problem arises.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some obligations are known and tracked, typically data protection, but the view is incomplete, unowned or out of date.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An owned, reviewed register of AI obligations guides design and approval, and each use records its regulatory role, duties, regulator contact and how obligations are shared.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Compliance with each obligation is checked and reported, and new or changed obligations are assessed for effect within a set time.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The organisation anticipates regulatory change, shapes its practice ahead of it, and contributes to consultations where it has relevant experience.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI obligations register with owners
- Per-use regulatory role and responsibility split record
