parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has adopted ethical principles for AI and applies them through a working review route that can change or stop a use of AI. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Adopted ethical principles for AI are applied through a defined review route with clear triggers.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The review route has authority to require changes to a use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The review route records its outcomes.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The review route is used across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use of AI is assessed against the adopted principles at the outset, and the result informs its approval tier.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Where principles conflict, the trade-off goes through the review route and is tested for necessity and proportionality.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each trade-off between principles is recorded with the alternatives considered and the reasons for the choice.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Many organisations publish principles that have no effect on what they build or buy. Principles only matter when there is a route that tests real proposals against them and has the authority to require changes.

Reaching Level 3:

- Adopt a short set of ethical principles for AI and get them approved.
- Set up a review route with clear triggers, recorded outcomes and authority to require changes or stop a use, and make it available across the organisation.
- Assess each use against the principles at the outset and use the result to set its approval tier (GOV-03).
- Where principles conflict, send the trade-off through the review route, test it for necessity and proportionality, and record the alternatives considered and the reasons.

Pitfalls:

- Publishing principles with no route that can change or stop a use.
- Resolving conflicts between principles informally, leaving no record of the trade-off.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What ethical principles has the organisation adopted for AI?
- Which proposals go to ethical review, and what can the review require?
- Can you give an example where ethical review changed or stopped a use of AI?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Record of trade-offs between principles, with alternatives and reasons
- The adopted principles and the terms of reference for the review route
- Records of ethical reviews and their outcomes
- Principles assessments at the outset and the approval tier they informed

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No adopted principles; ethical questions are left to individuals.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Principles are published, but there is no route for applying them to real cases, or the route is advisory and rarely used.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Adopted ethical principles are applied through a working review route with triggers and authority, used at the outset of each use and for recorded trade-offs.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Review outcomes are tracked to completion, the route's use and effect are reported, and cases that should have been reviewed but were not are identified.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Principles and the review route are refined from case experience and stakeholder feedback, and reasoning from past cases is reused as guidance.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Ethical principles statement
- Principles screening checklist for new uses
- Ethics review record including trade-off analysis

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Unfair bias is identified, tested for and reduced at each stage of a use of AI, from design through to live operation. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented approach to fairness and bias is applied across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each in-scope use of AI, the groups at risk and the fairness measures that matter are defined.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each in-scope use of AI is tested for fairness before release.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Fairness mitigations are recorded for each in-scope use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Fairness is monitored in live use through MON-02.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Proxies for protected characteristics are identified, and any use of them is recorded with reasons.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI can reproduce or amplify unfairness present in its data, its design or how it is used, and the effect often falls on groups already at a disadvantage. Bias needs managing across the lifecycle because it can appear after go-live as data and users change.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a fairness approach for the organisation explaining how groups at risk are identified, how fairness measures are chosen and how testing is done.
- For each in-scope use, define the groups at risk and the fairness measures that matter, and identify proxies for protected characteristics, recording any use of them with reasons.
- Test against the chosen measures before release and record the mitigations applied.
- Hand the fairness measures to live monitoring (MON-02) so they are tracked in use.

Pitfalls:

- Testing only overall accuracy, which can hide poor results for smaller groups.
- Removing protected characteristics but ignoring proxies that carry the same information.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a given use of AI, which groups could be treated unfairly, and how was that worked out?
- What testing for bias is done before release, and against what measures?
- How would you know if a live use started producing unfair results?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The documented approach to fairness and bias
- Bias test results and mitigation records for recent uses
- Live fairness monitoring reports

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Bias is not considered, or is assumed not to be present.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Bias is considered for some uses, usually at design, but testing is informal and live use is not checked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A documented fairness approach defines groups and measures for each in-scope use, tests before release, records mitigations and proxies, and monitors fairness in live use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Fairness breaches in live use lead to investigation, root-cause analysis and action, and fairness results are reported to the oversight forum.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Fairness methods are improved from monitoring results and external developments, and lessons are shared across uses.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Fairness approach document
- Per-use fairness test plan and results record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each use of AI has human oversight designed to match its risk, stating who reviews, at which point, and with what authority to override or stop it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For every use of AI, a documented oversight model, set according to risk, states who reviews, when, with what information, and their authority to override or stop the use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Reviewers are trained for their oversight role.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The oversight design is tested before go-live to show that reviewers can detect problems and intervene in time.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Agent actions that are consequential or hard to reverse need a person's approval before they take effect, and the oversight model lists which actions these are.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Putting a person in the loop does not help if they lack the time, information or authority to disagree with the system. Oversight has to be designed for each use so that human control is real where it is needed and not imposed as a formality where it adds nothing.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define a small set of oversight models (for example a person decides, a person reviews before action, a person monitors) and link each to risk tiers.
- For every use, document the chosen model, who reviews, when, with what information, and their authority to override or stop.
- Train reviewers for their role, including the limits of the AI and the risk of over-trusting it (see PPL-05).
- Test the oversight design before go-live to show reviewers can detect problems and intervene in time.

Pitfalls:

- Naming a reviewer who lacks the time, information or authority to intervene.
- Assuming oversight works without testing whether reviewers actually catch errors.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a given use of AI, who reviews its outputs, at what point, and can they override it?
- How was the level of oversight chosen, and how does it relate to the risk?
- How do you know reviewers are genuinely checking rather than approving by default?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- List of agent actions that need a person's approval, with approval records
- Documented oversight models for in-scope uses of AI
- Training records for people in oversight roles
- Override and review data from live uses

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Oversight is not designed; whether anyone checks AI outputs depends on the individual.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some uses have a human review step, but its purpose, timing and authority are not defined, or reviewers lack the information to challenge outputs.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every use of AI has a documented, risk-based oversight model with trained reviewers, tested before go-live to show they can detect problems and intervene.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Oversight is checked in practice, for example override rates and review times, and signs of rubber-stamping or overload are acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Oversight designs are refined from evidence of where human review adds value and where it does not.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Oversight model catalogue linked to risk tiers
- Per-use oversight design record
- Oversight test scenario pack

controls.title: Explanation and challenge for affected people

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: People affected by decisions that AI supports can find out that AI was involved, get an explanation they can understand, and challenge the outcome through a route that can change it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For every use of AI that supports decisions about people, those people are told that AI was involved.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People affected by such a decision can obtain a meaningful explanation of it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People affected by such a decision can challenge the outcome through a defined route with human review and authority to change it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People are told when they are interacting with AI, at first contact, clearly and accessibly, unless it is obvious.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People are told when they are exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, at first contact, clearly and accessibly, unless it is obvious.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
People are entitled to understand decisions made about them, and some have legal rights to do so. A working route to explanation and challenge also corrects individual errors and shows the organisation where a system is going wrong.

Reaching Level 3:

- Identify every use of AI that supports decisions about people.
- For each, write a clear notice telling people AI was involved, and set up a way for them to obtain a meaningful explanation.
- Set up a challenge route with human review and authority to change the outcome.
- Tell people clearly and accessibly at first contact when they are interacting with AI or are exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, unless it is obvious.

Pitfalls:

- Offering an explanation that describes the technology but not why this person got this outcome.
- Routing challenges to staff who cannot change the decision.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do people know when AI has contributed to a decision about them?
- What explanation can they get, and is it one a non-specialist can understand?
- How can they challenge an outcome, and how often do challenges succeed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Notices or communications telling people AI is involved
- The documented explanation and challenge route
- A log of challenges and their outcomes
- Notices shown to people at first contact with AI services

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Affected people are not told AI was involved and have no specific route to question the outcome.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Explanations or challenge are available for some uses, or on request only, and the route may not be able to change outcomes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: People know when AI is involved in decisions about them or in their interactions, can get a meaningful explanation, and can challenge outcomes through human review.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Requests for explanation and challenges are logged, outcomes and response times are measured, and patterns are fed back to the owners of the use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Explanation and challenge are designed in from the start, and the route is improved from the experience of the people who use it.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI involvement notice template
- Explanation and challenge procedure

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before AI in a bought product or service is used, and when it changes, the organisation assesses what it does, how it uses data, how the supplier changes the model, and what assurance the supplier offers. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A standard due diligence process covers AI in both new and existing bought products and services.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The due diligence covers function, data use, model change, content safeguards, energy use and wider sustainability practice, and supplier assurance.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Before AI from a supplier is used, its regulatory status is confirmed and the provider's instructions for use are obtained.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Due diligence confirms that AI from others is consistent with the organisation's adopted principles.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Due diligence results feed the risk assessment for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Supplier AI risk is reassessed on significant change and at set intervals.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: High-risk AI that is not registered where the law requires it is not used, and the provider or distributor is told.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Much of an organisation's AI arrives inside products it has bought, often switched on by a supplier update. The organisation carries the risk of that AI even though it did not build it, so it needs to understand it as well as it would its own.

Reaching Level 3:

- Build a due diligence questionnaire covering function, data use, model change, content safeguards, energy use and wider sustainability practice, assurance, and consistency with the adopted principles (RSK-05).
- Apply it to AI in new and existing products and services, confirming regulatory status and obtaining the provider's instructions for use before use.
- Do not use high-risk AI that is not registered where the law requires it, and tell the provider or distributor.
- Feed the results into the risk assessment for each use (RSK-02) and reassess on significant change and at set intervals.

Pitfalls:

- Checking only new purchases and missing AI added to existing products by supplier updates.
- Accepting supplier marketing claims as assurance without asking for evidence.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you find out whether a bought product or service contains AI, including after an update?
- What do you ask suppliers about how their AI works, uses your data and changes over time?
- What assurance do suppliers provide, and what happens when it is not enough?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The supplier AI due diligence questionnaire or process
- Completed due diligence records for recent purchases and updates
- Regulatory status checks and provider instructions for use, held for bought AI

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI in bought products is not identified or assessed; it is accepted as part of the product.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some suppliers are asked about AI, but questions are ad hoc, cover only new purchases, or miss updates that add AI to existing products.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Standard due diligence covers AI in new and existing bought products before use and at intervals, feeds each risk assessment, and keeps unregistered high-risk AI out.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Gaps in supplier assurance are tracked to closure and reported, and reassessment results inform renewal and purchasing decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Due diligence is refined from incidents and supplier experience, and the organisation's requirements shape what suppliers offer.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Supplier AI due diligence questionnaire
- Supplier AI reassessment schedule

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Covers how ideas for using AI are collected, ranked, tested and either scaled, stopped or retired. Treating uses of AI as a portfolio means effort goes to the uses most likely to pay off, weak ideas are stopped early and cheaply, and what works in one place is reused elsewhere.

controls.title: Idea intake open to all staff

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anyone in the organisation can propose a use of AI through a simple, well-known route, and every proposal is acknowledged and considered. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A single, documented intake route for proposing uses of AI is open to all staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The intake route is publicised across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The intake route has a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every proposal received through the route is acknowledged.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every proposal is logged in the pipeline register (POR-03).

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Many of the most useful ideas come from the people doing the work, not from a central team. Without an open route, ideas are lost, pursued quietly outside governance, or only come from those who already know the right people.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set up one simple intake route for AI ideas, such as a short form, and name its owner.
- Publicise the route to all staff through existing channels and AI learning material.
- Acknowledge every proposal and log it in the pipeline register (POR-03).

Pitfalls:

- Having several intake routes in different teams so ideas are duplicated or lost.
- Collecting ideas without telling proposers what happened to them.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How would a member of staff with an idea for using AI put it forward?
- What happens to a proposal once it is submitted, and how quickly does the proposer hear back?
- Which parts of the organisation do proposals come from, and which are missing?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The intake form or route, with its owner and how it is publicised
- A log of recent proposals showing acknowledgement and outcome

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No route for proposals; ideas progress only if someone senior or technical takes them up.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A route exists in some teams or functions, or is not widely known, and proposals are not always answered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Proposed uses of AI are ranked against published criteria covering value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit, applied the same way to every proposal. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Approved prioritisation criteria cover value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The prioritisation criteria are published.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The criteria are applied to every proposal.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The scoring and decision for each proposal are recorded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Demand for AI work usually exceeds the capacity to deliver it. Published criteria make choices explainable, stop the loudest voice winning, and keep the portfolio aligned with what the organisation is trying to achieve.

Reaching Level 3:

- Draft prioritisation criteria covering value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit, with a simple scoring scale.
- Get the criteria approved and publish them so proposers know how they will be judged.
- Apply the criteria to every proposal and record the scores and decision in the pipeline register (POR-03).

Pitfalls:

- Letting senior sponsorship override the scores without recording why.
- Using criteria so complex that small proposals cannot be scored quickly.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What criteria decide which proposals go ahead, and where are they published?
- Can you show how a recent proposal was scored and why it was or was not chosen?
- Have chosen uses delivered what their scores suggested?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The published prioritisation criteria and scoring method
- Scoring records for a sample of recent proposals

parts.name: level

parts.name: level

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Consistency of scoring is checked, and the realised value and cost of chosen uses are compared with their scores to test the criteria.

parts.title: Level 5: Optimising

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A single register records every proposed and in-flight use of AI with its status, owner and decision history, and hands each entry to the AI inventory when it goes live. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A single maintained register covers all proposed and in-flight uses of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each register entry records its status, owner, stage and decisions.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Uses are transferred from the register to the AI inventory (GOV-06) when they go live.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without a register, leaders cannot see what is being explored, duplicate work starts in different places, and decisions are hard to trace. A clean hand-over to the AI inventory (GOV-06) means nothing goes live without being recorded.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set up a single register for proposed and in-flight uses with fields for status, owner, stage and decisions.
- Name a register owner and make updating it part of every gate decision (POR-04).
- Transfer each use to the AI inventory (GOV-06) when it goes live.

Pitfalls:

- Keeping separate registers in each team so nobody sees the whole pipeline.
- Losing decision history when a use moves to the inventory.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Where can you see every use of AI currently proposed or being worked on?
- For a given entry, can you trace who decided what, and when?
- How does an entry move to the AI inventory when it goes live?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The pipeline register, with a recent update date
- Decision history for a sample of entries
- Examples of entries handed over to the AI inventory

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each use of AI passes through defined stages (explore, pilot, scale, operate, retire), with entry and exit criteria checked at each gate. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Documented stages for uses of AI have entry and exit criteria proportionate to risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The stages are applied to every use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Gate decisions are recorded in the pipeline register (POR-03).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A record of key design decisions and assumptions, with reasons, is kept for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The design record is updated at each gate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Gates give a consistent point to ask whether a use should continue, and they let effort and scrutiny grow as the use grows. Without them, pilots drift into live service without the checks that live service needs.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define stages for each use, such as explore, pilot, scale, operate and retire.
- Write entry and exit criteria for each stage, scaled to risk tier so low-risk uses move quickly.
- Apply the stages to every use and record each gate decision in the pipeline register (POR-03).
- Keep a record of key design decisions and assumptions, with reasons, for each use and update it at each gate.

Pitfalls:

- Applying the same heavy gates to every use regardless of risk.
- Recording gate outcomes but not the design decisions and assumptions behind them.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What stages does a use of AI pass through, and what must be true to pass each gate?
- Who decides at each gate, and where is the decision recorded?
- Have any uses reached live service without passing the expected gates?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Design decision record for each use, updated at each gate
- The documented stage-gate model with entry and exit criteria
- Gate decision records for a sample of uses

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No defined stages; work moves forward by default until someone stops it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Stages are described but criteria are vague or optional, or gates are used only for some uses.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Documented, risk-proportionate stages with entry and exit criteria apply to every use, with gate decisions and a running design record kept.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Gate outcomes and time spent at each stage are measured, and uses that skip or stall at a gate are identified and dealt with.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Gate criteria and stages are refined from evidence of which checks catch problems and which only add delay.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Stage gate criteria by risk tier
- Design decision and assumptions log template

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each use of AI has a business case scaled to its size and risk that states expected benefits, full costs and assumptions, and is approved before significant commitment. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A business case template is scaled by the size and risk of the use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every use of AI has a business case prepared with the template.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each business case states in plain language the problem the use solves, its benefits, one-off and running costs, assumptions, and options including not using AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each business case is approved at the right gate.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A business case forces the question of whether AI is the right answer and gives a baseline to judge the use against later. Making it proportionate stops small, low-risk uses being held up by paperwork meant for large investments.

Reaching Level 3:

- Create a business case template with a short version for small, low-risk uses and a fuller one for large or high-risk uses.
- Require each case to state in plain language the problem solved, benefits, one-off and running costs, assumptions and options, including not using AI.
- Set which gate approves the business case for each size and risk level (POR-04) and apply it to every use.

Pitfalls:

- Leaving out running costs such as usage charges and support (see OPM-03).
- Not considering a non-AI option, so AI is assumed to be the answer.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Does each use of AI have a business case, and how does its depth vary with size and risk?
- Does the case include running costs as well as set-up costs?
- When were the assumptions in a live use's case last checked?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The business case template and guidance on proportionality
- Approved business cases for a sample of uses of different sizes

parts.prose: Uses go ahead without a stated case; benefits are assumed rather than described.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Business cases are written for some uses, often large ones, but costs or benefits are incomplete or not quantified.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every use of AI has a plain-language business case, scaled by a template to its size and risk, covering problem, benefits, costs, assumptions and options, approved at a gate.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Business case assumptions are revisited at later gates, and cases that no longer hold lead to a recorded decision to continue, change or stop.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Estimates are calibrated against actual costs and benefits from past uses, so cases become more accurate over time.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Staff can try AI quickly within defined guardrails covering approved environments, data limits, time limits and exit criteria. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented experimentation route names the approved environments for trying AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The experimentation route sets rules on what data may be used.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The experimentation route sets time limits and exit criteria for experiments.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The experimentation route is available to all teams.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Teams use the experimentation route.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
People learn what AI can do by trying it, and blocking all experiments pushes them towards unapproved tools. Clear guardrails make fast trials possible while keeping sensitive data and live services out of reach until a use has been properly assessed.

Reaching Level 3:

- Provide one or more approved environments where staff can try AI tools safely (see TEC-01).
- Write simple rules on what data may and may not be used in experiments (see SEC-04 and DAT-05).
- Set a default time limit and exit criteria for each experiment, with a route into the pipeline (POR-03) if it succeeds.
- Document the route, make it available to all teams and check it is used.

Pitfalls:

- Making the route so slow that staff experiment with unapproved tools instead (see TEC-08).
- Allowing experiments to run on with no end date until they become live services by default.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- If a team wants to try an AI tool, where and how can they do it safely?
- What data may and may not be used in an experiment?
- How is an experiment ended, and what happens to its data and findings?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The experimentation rules, covering environments, data, time limits and exit
- A log of recent experiments with their start, end and outcome

parts.prose: Experiments are logged and checked against the guardrails, breaches are acted on, and the route's speed and take-up are measured.

parts.prose: Guardrails and environments are adjusted from what experiments reveal, so the route stays fast and safe as tools and needs change.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every pilot ends in a recorded decision to scale, extend or stop, made against criteria and evidence agreed before the pilot started. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every pilot has success and stop criteria agreed at the start.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every pilot ends in a recorded decision to scale, extend or stop.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each pilot decision is based on the evidence gathered in the pilot.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Pilots that are never formally ended either drift into live use without proper checks or linger and absorb effort. Agreeing success criteria in advance stops results being judged by enthusiasm after the event.

Reaching Level 3:

- Before each pilot starts, agree success and stop criteria and the evidence that will be gathered (see MON-01).
- Gather the evidence during the pilot as planned.
- End every pilot with a recorded scale, extend or stop decision based on the evidence, logged in the pipeline register (POR-03).

Pitfalls:

- Setting criteria after the pilot has run, so they fit the results.
- Extending pilots repeatedly to avoid making a decision.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What criteria were agreed before your most recent pilot began?
- How was the decision to scale, extend or stop it made, and by whom?
- Are any pilots running past their planned end without a decision?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Pilot plans showing success and stop criteria
- Recorded scale, extend or stop decisions with supporting evidence

parts.prose: Pilots continue or end by default; decisions are not recorded.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Some pilots have success criteria, but they are set late, loosely defined, or not used to decide.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every pilot has success and stop criteria agreed at the start and ends in a recorded, evidence-based decision to scale, extend or stop.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Pilot outcomes are tracked across the portfolio, extensions are time-limited and reviewed, and pilots running past their end date are flagged and resolved.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Decision criteria and pilot design are improved from how scaled uses perform in live service.

- Pilot decision record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Successful patterns, components and lessons from uses of AI are recorded so others can find them, and are reused before anything new is built. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Reusable patterns, components and lessons from uses of AI are recorded in a known place.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: New proposals are checked against the recorded patterns, components and lessons before work starts.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each shared component has a named owner responsible for its upkeep and documentation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Different teams often face the same problem. Reuse cuts cost and time, spreads approaches already assessed and approved, and avoids several slightly different solutions that each need supporting.

Reaching Level 3:

- Choose one known place to record reusable patterns, components and lessons, and tell staff about it.
- Give each shared component a named owner responsible for its upkeep and documentation.
- Add a check at intake or the first gate (POR-01, POR-04) that new proposals are compared against what already exists before work starts.

Pitfalls:

- Recording components with no owner, so they go out of date and nobody trusts them.
- Sharing only successes and not the lessons from what failed (see CUL-05).

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Where would a team look to see whether a similar use of AI already exists?
- Is checking for reuse part of how new proposals are assessed?
- Can you give an example where something built for one use was reused elsewhere?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The catalogue or library of reusable patterns, components and lessons
- Proposal or gate records showing the reuse check

parts.prose: Each team starts from scratch; reuse happens only through personal contacts.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some patterns or components are shared, but there is no place to find them and no expectation to look.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Reusable patterns, components and lessons are recorded in a known place, checked before new work starts, and each shared component has an owner.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The amount of reuse and the effort it saves are measured, and proposals that duplicate existing work are caught at intake or the first gate.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Assets are designed for reuse from the start, and the reuse library is curated and improved from how it is used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Uses of AI that no longer earn their place are withdrawn through a planned process that covers users, dependent processes and disposal or retention of models and data. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented retirement process is triggered by periodic review of live uses of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The retirement process covers user transition, dependent processes, records, and disposal or retention of models and data.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The retirement process covers reuse, recycling or disposal of dedicated hardware and infrastructure.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each retirement updates the AI inventory (GOV-06).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The effect of a withdrawal on affected people and services is assessed, and groups at greater risk are identified.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Users and affected people are told about a withdrawal in advance.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI that stays in use after it stops delivering costs money, carries risk and may give worse results as conditions change. Unplanned withdrawal leaves users stranded and leaves models and data behind with nobody accountable for them.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set a periodic review of live uses that asks whether each still earns its place and triggers retirement if not.
- Write a retirement process covering user transition, dependent processes, records, disposal or retention of models and data, and reuse, recycling or disposal of dedicated hardware and infrastructure.
- Assess the effect of withdrawal on affected people and services, identify groups at greater risk, and tell users and affected people in advance.
- Update the AI inventory (GOV-06) when a use is retired.

Pitfalls:

- Switching off a use without checking which processes depend on it.
- Keeping models and data indefinitely after retirement with no retention decision (see DAT-06).

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you decide that a use of AI should be retired?
- When a use was last retired, what happened to its users, models and data?
- Are there uses still running that nobody would miss?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Withdrawal impact assessment and notice to users and affected people for each retired use
- The retirement process and its triggers
- Records of a completed retirement, including data and model disposal
- AI inventory entries marked as retired

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Live uses are routinely reviewed against retirement triggers, retirements are checked for completion, and leftover models or data are found and dealt with.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Retirement is planned from the design stage, and the process is refined from lessons of past withdrawals.

parts.prose: Covers who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, how sourcing choices are made, how running costs and suppliers are managed, and the standards delivery teams work to. A clear operating model lets AI move from pilot to dependable service without every team inventing its own way of working.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has a defined, approved operating model that states who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, and what is done centrally and what locally. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved operating model for AI is documented.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The model states which parts of building, buying, running and supporting AI are done centrally and which locally.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each of these activities has a named responsible team with the resources to carry it out.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The interfaces between central and local teams are defined.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: AI work across the organisation follows the model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without an agreed model, central teams and business units duplicate effort, compete for the same scarce skills, or each assume the other is responsible. Whether the model is central, devolved or hub-and-spoke matters less than everyone knowing which it is.

Reaching Level 3:

- Map who currently builds, buys, runs and supports AI, including work happening in business units without central involvement.
- Choose a model (central, devolved or hub-and-spoke) and write down which of those four activities sit centrally and which locally.
- Name the team responsible for each activity, the people and budget behind it, and how central and local teams hand work to each other.
- Get the model approved by the executive sponsor (GOV-02), give it an owner and review date, and update team remits to match.
- Tell every business unit how to route AI work through the model and check new work against it.

Pitfalls:

- Writing a model on paper while the people and money stay where they were, so nobody follows it.
- Covering building and buying but forgetting who runs and supports AI once it is live.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which teams build, buy, run and support AI, and where is that written down?
- What is done centrally and what is left to business units?
- Where is AI work happening outside the agreed model?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved operating model document, with owner and review date
- Team remits or service catalogue entries that reflect the model

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: A consistent, documented method decides for each use of AI whether to configure tools already owned, procure, build, or wait, and the reasons are recorded. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented sourcing method covers the options to configure existing tools, procure, build or wait.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The method sets decision criteria, such as cost, speed, control, skills, lock-in and environmental footprint.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The method is applied to every use of AI and each sourcing decision is recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Reuse of existing and openly available models is considered before any new model is trained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI capability is increasingly built into products the organisation already pays for, so building or buying something new is often unnecessary. A consistent method weighs cost, speed, control, skills and lock-in, and avoids choices driven by habit or by whichever supplier asked first.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a short decision method with four routes: configure tools already owned, procure, build, or wait.
- Set criteria for choosing between them, covering cost, speed, control, skills, lock-in and environmental footprint.
- Require teams to check whether an existing or openly available model can be reused before proposing to train a new one.
- Apply the method to every proposed use and record the route chosen and the reasons, for example in the pipeline register (POR-03).

Pitfalls:

- Skipping the configure and wait options because a supplier is already pitching a new product.
- Recording the decision but not the reasons, so it cannot be reviewed later.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How was the sourcing route chosen for your most recent use of AI?
- Is configuring tools you already own considered before buying or building?
- Have past sourcing choices turned out as expected on cost and support?

parts.prose:
- The sourcing method or decision guide
- Recorded sourcing decisions for a sample of uses

parts.prose: The ongoing cost of each AI service, including usage-based charges, is known, forecast, assigned to an owner and kept within agreed limits. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.prose: Actual running costs are tracked for every AI service.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Running costs are forecast for every AI service.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The running costs of each AI service are assigned to a named budget holder.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Usage limits or cost alerts are set for each AI service.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Running costs are reviewed against budget on a set cycle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI services are often priced by usage, so costs can grow quickly and unpredictably as adoption spreads. Costs that nobody watches can erode the benefits a use was approved for, or lead to abrupt withdrawal when the money runs out.

Reaching Level 3:

- List every AI service, including licences and usage-priced services, and assign each to a named budget holder.
- Set up tracking so the running cost of each service can be seen separately each month.
- Forecast the cost of each service for the year ahead, using expected growth in use.
- Set usage limits or spending alerts on usage-priced services, at levels agreed with the budget holder.
- Review actual cost against budget and forecast on a fixed cycle, and adjust limits or forecasts as needed.

Pitfalls:

- Tracking licence costs but missing charges that rise with use, such as per-request pricing.
- Setting alerts that go to a shared inbox nobody reads.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What does each AI service cost to run each month, and who owns that cost?
- What stops usage-based charges rising beyond budget without anyone noticing?
- How do actual running costs compare with what the business case assumed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Cost reports by AI service, with budget holders
- Usage limits, alerts or forecasts in place for usage-priced services

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Costs are tracked for some services, but forecasts, usage limits or cost owners are missing.

parts.name: level

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Cost data shapes design and sourcing choices, and pricing models are renegotiated or changed from evidence of how services are used.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Contracts for AI products and services set clear terms on data rights, intellectual property, notice of model changes, transparency and exit. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Standard AI contract terms exist and are used in every relevant procurement.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms used in each procurement are informed by the supplier risk assessment (RSK-09).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms cover data use and rights, and intellectual property in inputs and outputs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms require notice of model changes and the transparency information the organisation needs, including what it must publish about the use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms set security requirements and the split of security responsibilities between the parties.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms give incident notification, access to the logs the organisation needs, and a right to audit or accepted independent assurance.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms cover operational resilience and exit, including data format, retention, return and deletion.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The terms allocate responsibility and liability for AI outputs and any harm they cause.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Standard technology contracts often say nothing about how a supplier may use the organisation's data, who owns outputs, or what happens when the underlying model changes. Settling these terms at procurement is far easier than trying to add them once the service is in use.

Reaching Level 3:

- Draft a standard AI contract schedule covering data use and rights, intellectual property in inputs and outputs, notice of model changes, transparency information needed for publication, and exit.
- Add security terms: security requirements and the split of responsibilities, incident notification, access to logs, a right to audit or accepted independent assurance, and operational resilience.
- Make the exit terms state data format, retention, return and deletion, and set out who is responsible and liable for AI outputs and any harm they cause.
- Require the supplier risk assessment (RSK-09) to be done first and use its findings to decide which terms need strengthening.
- Make the schedule a required part of every procurement that involves AI, and brief the people who run procurements.

Pitfalls:

- Using the schedule only for large purchases while AI features arrive through renewals of existing products.
- Accepting a supplier's standard terms on model changes, which often allow change without notice.
- Leaving liability for wrong or harmful outputs unaddressed.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What does your standard contract say about the supplier's use of your data?
- Will the supplier tell you before changing the model behind the service?
- Who owns the outputs, and what happens to your data when the contract ends?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Standard AI contract clauses or schedule
- A sample of recent AI contracts showing those terms

parts.name: level

parts.name: level

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI suppliers are managed against agreed performance measures, and each critical AI service has a tested route to exit or replace the supplier. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every AI supplier has a named owner in the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every AI supplier has agreed performance measures that are reviewed on a set cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each critical AI service has a documented exit plan covering data return and replacement.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI suppliers change their models, pricing and products often, and some may withdraw altogether. Regular performance management catches decline early, and a workable exit route stops the organisation being tied to a supplier that no longer serves it.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name an owner for every AI supplier relationship.
- Agree performance measures with each supplier, such as availability, response times, accuracy or support quality.
- Hold supplier reviews against those measures on a fixed cycle and record the outcome.
- Identify which AI services are critical and write an exit plan for each, covering how data is returned and what would replace the service.

Pitfalls:

- Treating exit planning as a contract clause rather than a plan someone could follow.
- Measuring only availability when the supplier's model quality is what matters to users.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Who manages each AI supplier, and what measures are they held to?
- If a critical AI supplier withdrew its service, what would you do and how long would it take?
- Has any exit plan been tested?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Supplier performance reports and review records
- Exit plans for critical AI services, with any test results

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Suppliers are not actively managed once the contract is signed; there is no exit plan.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some suppliers are reviewed, but measures are informal and exit plans are missing or untested.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every AI supplier has an owner and agreed performance measures reviewed regularly, and each critical AI service has a documented exit plan.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Supplier performance is reported and acted on, and exit plans for critical services are tested or rehearsed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Supplier management and exit planning are refined from experience of supplier changes and exits.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI work is delivered by multidisciplinary teams using user-centred methods to defined delivery standards. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Documented delivery standards for AI exist and are applied to all AI delivery.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The standards require multidisciplinary teams, user research and iterative testing with users.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The standards include AI-specific engineering practice and the design of how people and AI share work.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Delivery teams include subject matter experts for the data and the work, involved in design and evaluation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The standards require safety, security and privacy by design, with privacy-protective default settings.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Accuracy, robustness and reliability requirements are set at design for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Diversity of perspective is considered for each team, including contracted third parties, and structured stakeholder input is added where it falls short.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Services, documentation and notices are tested with users who have accessibility needs before go-live.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI that works technically can still fail in use if it does not fit how people work. Teams that bring together users, business, data, technical and risk knowledge, and that test with real users as they go, are more likely to build something people adopt.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write AI delivery standards requiring multidisciplinary teams that include subject matter experts for the data and the work, user research and iterative testing with users, and AI engineering practice.
- Include in the standards how people and AI share work, safety, security and privacy by design with protective defaults, and accuracy, robustness and reliability requirements set at design.
- Require each team to check its diversity of perspective, including contractors, and to seek structured stakeholder input where it falls short; research with people follows OPM-10.
- Require testing of services, documentation and notices with users who have accessibility needs before go-live, and apply the standards to all AI delivery.

Pitfalls:

- Bringing users in only at the end to accept something already built.
- Leaving accessibility testing until after launch.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Who is in the team delivering a use of AI, and how are users involved?
- What delivery standards apply to AI work, and how is compliance checked?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The delivery standards or playbook for AI work
- Team composition and user research records for a sample of projects
- Accessibility test records from before go-live

parts.name: level

parts.prose: AI work is done by technical staff alone, with little contact with users.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Some projects use multidisciplinary teams or user research, but there is no common standard.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Documented delivery standards for multidisciplinary, user-centred AI delivery, with safety, security, privacy, accessibility and quality built in from design, are applied to all AI delivery.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Delivery is checked against the standards at gates, and user adoption and satisfaction are measured and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Delivery standards are improved from user outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every live AI service has defined support, change and problem management arrangements, including handling of changes to models and prompts. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every live AI service has a named support owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Users of each live AI service have a route to report problems.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Change management for each live AI service covers changes to the model, prompts, data and hosting platform.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Problem management covers each live AI service, including problems arising from model, prompt, data and hosting platform changes.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Once live, AI needs the same support as any other service, plus extra care because its behaviour can change when models, prompts or data change. Without service management, problems go unreported and changes reach users untested.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name a support owner for every live AI service and add each service to the service catalogue.
- Give users a clear route to report problems with each service, using the existing service desk where there is one.
- Extend change management so that changes to models, prompts, data and the hosting platform are recorded, assessed and approved before they reach users.
- Bring AI problems into problem management so repeat faults are investigated, with release and rollback detail handled under TEC-05.

Pitfalls:

- Missing changes made by the supplier to the underlying model, which arrive without a change request.
- Leaving prompt edits outside change control because they look minor.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- If a user finds a problem with a live AI service, where do they report it?
- How are changes to the model or prompts behind a service approved and tested?
- Who supports each live AI service out of hours, if needed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Service catalogue or support records for live AI services
- Change records covering model or prompt updates

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Live AI is supported informally by whoever built it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some services are in the support process, but AI-specific changes such as model or prompt updates are not covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every live AI service has a support owner, a problem reporting route for users, and change and problem management that covers AI-specific changes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Service levels, problems and changes are measured and reported, and repeat problems lead to root cause fixes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Service management practice for AI is refined from incident and change data and from user feedback.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation works with peer organisations and partners to share AI solutions, lessons and capacity where this serves its aims. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A stated approach to collaboration exists and says which kinds of partner are sought and why.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The organisation takes part in relevant peer groups or partnerships.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Solutions and lessons are shared and taken up within agreed rules on data and intellectual property.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Partnership agreements state the adopted ethical principles and the data and intellectual property terms.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Many organisations face the same AI problems. Sharing solutions and lessons reduces cost and repeated mistakes, and pooled capacity gives smaller organisations access to skills they could not hold alone.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a short collaboration approach that says which kinds of partner the organisation seeks and why.
- Join one or more relevant peer groups or partnerships and name who represents the organisation.
- Agree rules for sharing data and intellectual property before sharing solutions or lessons.
- Make sure each partnership agreement states the ethical principles adopted (RSK-05) and the data and intellectual property terms.
- Record solutions and lessons shared with and taken up from partners.

Pitfalls:

- Relying on personal contacts, so collaboration stops when one person leaves.
- Sharing material before agreeing who owns it and how it may be used.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which peer organisations or partners do you work with on AI, and on what?
- Can you give an example of a solution or lesson you shared or took up?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Membership or partnership records and agreements
- Examples of solutions or lessons shared or reused
- Partnership agreements stating principles, data and intellectual property terms

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Collaboration shapes the organisation's AI plans, and it contributes to and learns from shared work as a matter of course.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Services that depend on AI can continue safely when the AI is unavailable, degraded or producing wrong results, through planned fallbacks that have been tested. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An impact analysis of AI unavailability exists for each service that depends on AI and sets its recovery objectives.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each such service has a documented fallback or safe stop, based on the impact analysis, covering unavailability, degradation and wrong output.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Fallbacks and safe stops are included in continuity plans.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Fallbacks are tested on a set cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Users and affected parties are told when a fallback or safe stop is in force.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI services fail in ways other systems do not, including supplier outages, model changes and confident but wrong output. Services that rely on AI need a planned way to carry on, or to stop safely, so that a failure does not become harm to the people they serve.

Reaching Level 3:

- List every service that depends on AI, using the AI inventory (GOV-06).
- Analyse the impact of the AI being unavailable for each service and set recovery objectives from that analysis.
- Document a fallback or safe stop for each service that covers the AI being unavailable, degraded or producing wrong output, and add it to continuity plans.
- Prepare how users and affected parties will be told when a fallback or safe stop is in force.
- Test each fallback on a fixed cycle and record the results and actions.

Pitfalls:

- Planning only for outages and not for the AI giving confident but wrong answers.
- Assuming staff can return to the manual process when the skills or capacity to do so have gone.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which services depend on AI, and what happens to each if the AI stops or gets things wrong?
- Are AI dependencies included in business continuity plans?
- When were the fallbacks last tested, and what did the test show?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Impact analysis of AI unavailability with recovery objectives for each dependent service
- Continuity plans or service designs showing AI dependencies and fallbacks
- Fallback test records with results and actions

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Dependence on AI is not considered in continuity planning; a failure would be handled when it happened.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Some services have fallbacks, but they are informal, untested or do not cover degraded or wrong output.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every service that depends on AI has a tested fallback or safe stop, based on an impact analysis and part of continuity plans, and people are told when it is used.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Recovery times are measured against targets, and failures in testing are fixed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Continuity is improved from tests, incidents and supplier changes, and the degree of dependence on AI is set deliberately for each service.

parts.name: artefacts

- AI dependency impact analysis with recovery objectives
- Fallback and safe stop plan per service
- Fallback test record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Evaluations and research that involve people have their informed consent, ethics review and protection, use participants who represent those the service will serve, and for significant uses draw on the communities affected. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Evaluations and user research involving people have the informed consent of participants.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Evaluations and user research involving people go through ethics review by the organisation's established route.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Participants represent the people the service will serve.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Research with participants protects their wellbeing and their right to withdraw.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For significant uses, affected communities and experts who are not users are engaged at planning and design, and their input and the organisation's response are recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Research and evaluation plans assess and manage risks to the physical and emotional safety of the researchers as well as the participants.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Testing AI with people gives the best evidence of how it will work in use, but it puts those people at some risk and is only useful if they reflect the people the service will serve. Engaging affected communities early on significant uses brings concerns to light while the design can still change.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set rules for research with people: informed consent, and ethics review through the organisation's existing route.
- Recruit participants who represent the people the service will serve, and protect their wellbeing and their right to withdraw.
- For significant uses, engage affected communities and experts who are not users at planning and design, and record their input and the response.
- Build these rules into the delivery standards (OPM-06) so every team applies them.

Pitfalls:

- Treating ethics review and consent as optional for internal pilots that still involve people.
- Engaging communities only after the design is fixed, so their input cannot change it.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do evaluations and user research involving people get informed consent and ethics review?
- How do you make sure participants represent the people the service will serve, and that their wellbeing and right to withdraw are protected?
- For significant uses, which affected communities and outside experts were engaged at planning and design, and what was done with their input?
- How are researchers kept safe, for example when research covers sensitive topics?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Consent and ethics review records for evaluations involving people
- Participant recruitment records showing how representation was sought
- Engagement records for significant uses, with the input received and the organisation's response
- Research plans showing the risk assessment for researchers

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Research and evaluation with people happen informally, without consent records or ethics review.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some projects obtain consent or ethics review, but there is no common standard, participants are chosen for convenience, or affected communities are not engaged.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Evaluations and research involving people have informed consent, ethics review, representative participants and protection of wellbeing and the right to withdraw, and significant uses engage affected communities at planning and design.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Consent, ethics review and participant representation are checked at delivery gates, and community input and the response to it are reviewed for significant uses.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Research practice and community engagement are improved from participant feedback, outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

- Consent form and participant information template
- Stakeholder engagement record

parts.prose: Covers the data and information that AI uses and produces: who owns it, whether it is good enough for the job, whether its use is lawful and fair, whether people can find and understand it, how long it is kept, who can reach it and where it came from. Most problems with AI in use trace back to data, so these controls apply to bought and embedded AI as much as to anything built in-house.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation's data strategy states what its planned uses of AI need from data and sets out how those needs will be met. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved data strategy exists with an owner and a review date.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The strategy sets out what planned uses of AI need from data.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The strategy sets out the actions and funding to meet those needs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An approved data architecture covers how data used by AI is taken in, stored, organised and maintained.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Shared definitions are in place for the data used by AI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI ambitions often assume data that does not exist, cannot be joined up or is not allowed to be used. Writing AI's needs into the data strategy brings those gaps into view early, and lets data investment be planned alongside AI investment rather than after it.

Reaching Level 3:

- Gather what the planned uses of AI need from data, drawing on the AI strategy (STR-01) and roadmap (STR-06).
- Compare those needs with the data held today and list the gaps.
- Set out actions and funding to close the gaps in the data strategy, and get it approved with an owner and review date.
- Document a data architecture showing how data used by AI is taken in, stored, organised and maintained, with shared definitions for key terms, and get it approved.

Pitfalls:

- Writing the data strategy in general terms without naming the AI uses it serves.
- Agreeing actions with no funding attached.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Does the data strategy say what your planned uses of AI need from data?
- Which data gaps are holding back AI today, and who is closing them?
- When the AI roadmap changes, how does the data strategy change with it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved data strategy, with the sections covering AI needs
- A data action plan or roadmap linked to the AI roadmap, with owners and progress
- The approved data architecture

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No data strategy, or one that does not mention AI; data needs are discovered project by project.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: The data strategy mentions AI in general terms, but does not state what data AI needs or how gaps will be closed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An approved, owned data strategy sets out what planned AI needs from data and the actions and funding to meet it, backed by an approved data architecture.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progress against the data actions that AI depends on is measured and reported, and slippage that puts AI plans at risk is escalated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The data strategy and the AI strategy are revised together, using evidence of which data constraints have most limited AI value.

- Data architecture diagram and description
- Shared data definitions list

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Every data set used by AI has a named accountable owner and day-to-day stewards who understand the data and look after it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every data set used by AI has a named owner and a named steward.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Owners and stewards are recorded in a central record.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Owner and steward responsibilities for approving use, quality and access are defined.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Decisions about whether data can be used for AI, whether it is good enough and who may see it need someone with authority to make them. Without named owners and stewards these questions go unanswered, or are answered by whoever happens to be building the system.

Reaching Level 3:

- List every data set used by AI, starting from the AI inventory (GOV-06).
- Name an accountable owner and a day-to-day steward for each data set.
- Write down what owners and stewards are responsible for, including approving use, quality and access.
- Record owners and stewards in one central place, such as the data catalogue (DAT-04), and keep it current when people move.

Pitfalls:

- Naming a team or system as owner rather than a person.
- Giving people the title without the time or authority to do the job.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For the data a given use of AI depends on, who is the owner and who looks after it day to day?
- What can the owner decide, and what must they be asked about before the data is used for AI?
- What happens to ownership when the owner changes role or the data set changes?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- A register of data owners and stewards covering data used by AI
- Role descriptions or terms of reference setting out owner and steward responsibilities
- Examples of owners approving or declining a use of their data

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Ownership of data is unclear; system administrators or project teams make decisions about data by default.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some important data sets have named owners, but stewardship is informal and data used by AI is not consistently covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every data set used by AI has a named owner and steward, recorded centrally, with defined responsibilities for approving use, quality and access.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Coverage of ownership and stewardship is measured, gaps are filled within a set time, and owners are held to their responsibilities through regular review.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Owners and stewards actively shape how their data is used for AI, and the arrangements are improved from experience of where decisions were slow or missed.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Data owner and steward register
- Role descriptions for data owner and steward

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The quality of data used by each AI system is assessed against what that use needs, and shortfalls are fixed or their effects managed before and during live use. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Quality requirements, including relevance and representativeness for the intended purpose, are set for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Data is assessed against those requirements before use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Data is reassessed against those requirements at intervals during use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each quality shortfall has an owner and a remediation or mitigation plan.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI reproduces the gaps, errors and skews in its data, often at scale and with confidence. Quality is relative to the use: data adequate for monthly reporting may be unfit for an automated decision about an individual.

Reaching Level 3:

- For each use of AI, set quality requirements for its data, including relevance and representativeness for the intended purpose.
- Assess the data against those requirements before use and record the result.
- Reassess at set intervals while the AI is live.
- Give every shortfall an owner and a plan to fix it or reduce its effect.

Pitfalls:

- Checking completeness and accuracy but not whether the data represents the people or cases the AI will meet.
- Assessing quality once before launch and never again.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What quality does this use of AI need from its data, and who decided that?
- When was the data last assessed against those requirements, and what did it find?
- What happens when data quality drops while the system is live?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Data quality requirements for a sample of uses of AI
- Data quality assessment results and the remediation actions that followed

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Data quality is assumed; problems are found when outputs look wrong.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Quality is checked for some uses or some data sets, without agreed measures or a link to what the AI use needs.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Quality requirements are set for each use of AI, data is assessed against them before and during use, and shortfalls are owned and remediated or mitigated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Quality measures are tracked over time for data used by AI, falls below threshold trigger action, and the effect of quality on AI outputs is understood.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Quality issues are fixed at source, and requirements and checks are refined from evidence of which quality problems most affected AI outcomes.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Data quality requirements per use
- Data quality assessment record
- Shortfall and remediation log
