parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Data available for AI is catalogued and described well enough that people can find it, understand what it means and its limits, and use it correctly. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A maintained catalogue covers data used or available for AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each catalogue entry records the owner, meaning, coverage, known limits and conditions of use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each catalogue entry records its sensitivity classification and whether it holds personal data.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Teams that cannot find suitable data either give up or use the wrong data. Descriptions of meaning, coverage and known limits stop data being used for purposes it does not support, which is a common cause of misleading AI outputs.

Reaching Level 3:

- Choose a catalogue tool or a simple shared register, and give it an owner.
- Add every data set used or available for AI, recording owner, meaning, coverage, known limits and conditions of use.
- Record each entry's sensitivity classification and whether it holds personal data.
- Set a routine for owners or stewards (DAT-02) to keep entries current.

Pitfalls:

- Building a large catalogue that nobody maintains, so it goes out of date within months.
- Leaving out known limits, which are what stop data being misused.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How would a team planning a new use of AI find out what data exists and whether they can use it?
- For a data set used by AI, where are its meaning, coverage and known limits written down?
- How do you know the catalogue is complete and current?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The data catalogue, with sample entries for data used by AI
- The process for adding and updating catalogue entries

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Knowledge of what data exists sits with individuals; finding data means asking around.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some data sets are listed or documented, but descriptions are incomplete, out of date or held in separate places.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A maintained catalogue describes data used or available for AI, including its owner, meaning, limits, conditions of use and sensitivity.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Catalogue completeness and accuracy are measured, and use of the catalogue is tracked to show whether people find what they need.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Catalogue entries are kept current largely as a by-product of normal data work, and descriptions are improved from feedback by the people using them.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Data catalogue or register
- Catalogue entry template

controls.title: Lawful and fair use of data

props.name: cross-reference

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before data is used in an AI system, its use is confirmed as lawful, consistent with the purpose for which it was collected, and fair to the people it describes. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use of data in AI has a record of its lawful basis, purpose compatibility check and fairness consideration.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each record is completed before use and signed off by the data owner with data protection advice.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Data collected and processed for each use is limited to what the purpose needs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Wherever personal data is used, including to train or tune AI, privacy enhancing techniques such as minimisation, anonymisation or synthetic data are considered, informed by the impact assessment, and the decision is recorded with reasons.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People whose data or inputs an AI system uses are told, accessibly, how they are used, accessed and stored, including any retraining and review by staff or suppliers.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Individual rights requests about data used in AI are handled, including where personal data has been used to train a model.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Using existing data for AI is often a new purpose that the original basis for holding it does not cover. Settling the lawful basis and fairness of each use before work starts avoids systems that have to be withdrawn, and protects the people whose data is used.

Reaching Level 3:

- Before each use of data in AI, record the lawful basis, a check that the use fits the purpose the data was collected for, and a fairness consideration, signed off by the data owner with data protection advice.
- Limit the data collected and processed to what the purpose needs, and record the decision on privacy enhancing techniques such as minimisation, anonymisation or synthetic data, with reasons informed by the impact assessment (RSK-03).
- Tell people, in accessible language, how their data or inputs are used, accessed and stored, including any retraining and any review by staff or suppliers.
- Set up a route to handle individual rights requests, including where personal data has been used to train a model.

Pitfalls:

- Seeking data protection advice only after the system is built.
- Having no answer for a rights request about data already used to train a model.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a given use of AI, what is the lawful basis for using each data set, and where is it recorded?
- Was the data collected for a purpose compatible with this use?
- When is this checked again, for example when the system or its data changes?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Recorded decision on privacy enhancing techniques for each training or tuning data set that holds personal data
- Records of lawful basis, purpose compatibility and fairness for a sample of uses of AI
- Data protection advice or sign-off on those uses
- Notices telling people how their data and inputs are used, accessed and stored

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Data is used for AI wherever it is available; lawful basis and fairness are not considered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Data protection advice is sought for some uses, usually late or only for obviously personal data.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Each use of data in AI has a lawful basis, purpose check and fairness consideration signed off before use, with data minimised and privacy techniques considered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: These records are checked for completeness against the AI inventory, are revisited when the use or the data changes, and gaps are acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Lawful and fair use is designed in from the start of each use of AI, and the approach is refined from case outcomes, complaints and changes in law.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Data use assessment template
- Privacy notice wording for AI uses
- Rights request procedure covering trained models

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Retention and records rules cover what AI systems take in and produce, including prompts, outputs and the decisions they supported, and are applied in practice. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Records and retention rules state how AI inputs, prompts, outputs and supported decisions are classified, kept, made retrievable and deleted.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The rules cover system logs and keep them for at least as long as the law requires.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The rules are applied to every use of AI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI creates new kinds of information that may need to be kept as evidence of a decision, disclosed on request, or deleted on time. If records rules do not cover them, the organisation can neither explain past decisions nor show it is not keeping data longer than it should.

Reaching Level 3:

- Extend the records and retention schedule to cover AI inputs, prompts, outputs and the decisions they supported.
- Set for each how it is classified, how long it is kept, how it can be retrieved and how it is deleted.
- Include system logs, kept at least as long as the law requires (see RSK-04 for the obligations).
- Apply the rules to every use of AI and check that retrieval works in practice.

Pitfalls:

- Keeping AI outputs but not the prompts or inputs that produced them, so decisions cannot be reconstructed.
- Leaving supplier-held logs outside the rules.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Are prompts and outputs from your AI tools treated as records, and under which rules?
- If asked to show how an AI-supported decision was reached a year ago, what could you retrieve?
- Who checks that retention settings in bought AI tools match your rules?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Retention schedule or records policy entries covering AI inputs, outputs and decisions
- Configuration records showing retention settings in AI tools
- Results of a retrieval or deletion check
- Retention settings for AI system logs

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No one has considered whether AI inputs and outputs are records; retention depends on product defaults.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some rules exist for some AI systems, but prompts, outputs and AI-supported decisions are not consistently covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Records and retention rules cover AI inputs, prompts, outputs, supported decisions and system logs, and are applied to every use of AI.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Application of the rules is checked, including retention settings in bought tools, and failures such as unretrievable records or late deletion are caught and fixed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Records handling for AI is largely automated, and the rules are refined from requests for information, audits and changes in how AI is used.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI records and retention schedule
- Retrieval test record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI systems and their users can reach only the data they need for the agreed purpose, and data is shared into and out of AI systems only under agreed rules. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Access by each AI system and its users is limited to what the agreed purpose needs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Access by each AI system and its users is approved by the data owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Sharing data with other systems or organisations follows documented agreements.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented route exists for requesting access to data for AI work.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Live personal or sensitive data is used in development, test or experimentation only with data owner approval.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Live personal or sensitive data used in development, test or experimentation is minimised or protected.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI systems are often given broad access to make them work quickly, and then surface data to users who would never have been allowed to see it directly. Applying least privilege and sharing rules to the AI system itself, not only to its users, keeps existing permissions meaningful.

Reaching Level 3:

- For each AI system, define the data it and its users need for the agreed purpose and limit access to that, with data owner approval.
- Put sharing with other systems or organisations under documented agreements.
- Publish a route for requesting access to data for AI work.
- Require data owner approval before live personal or sensitive data is used in development, test or experimentation, and minimise or protect it when it is.

Pitfalls:

- Giving an AI system broad service account access because it is easier to set up.
- Copying live data into test environments without approval.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What data can this AI system reach, and could a user obtain through it something they could not see directly?
- Who approved that access, and when was it last reviewed?
- Where data is shared with another organisation or service for AI, what agreement covers it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Access approvals and the latest access review for a sample of AI systems
- Data sharing agreements covering AI use

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI systems are given whatever access makes them work; sharing happens without agreed rules.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Access is restricted for some systems or data, but AI systems' own access is not reviewed and sharing rules are informal.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Access to data by AI systems and users is limited to the agreed purpose and approved, sharing follows agreements, and live sensitive data in development is controlled.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Access rights and sharing agreements for AI are reviewed on a set cycle, excess access is removed, and breaches of sharing rules are detected and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Access and sharing controls for AI are applied automatically from data classification and purpose, and are refined from review findings.

- Access approval record per AI system
- Data sharing agreement template
- Data access request form

controls.title: Provenance of training and test data

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For data used to train, tune or test AI, the organisation knows and records where it came from, what rights it holds over it, and any limits on its use. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For every data set used to train, tune or test AI, the source, collection method, rights, licence terms and use limits are recorded before use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each such data set is linked to the models that used it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The preparation and labelling steps applied to each such data set are recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Synthetic and augmented data are labelled as such, with a record of how they were generated and how their fitness was checked.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Data of unknown origin can carry rights the organisation does not hold, biases nobody can trace, or restrictions that surface only after release. A recorded provenance lets these questions be answered, and lets a model be rebuilt or withdrawn if a source turns out to be unusable.

Reaching Level 3:

- Before any data set is used to train, tune or test AI, record its source, collection method, rights, licence terms and use limits.
- Record the preparation and labelling steps applied to each data set.
- Label synthetic and augmented data as such, and record how it was generated and how its fitness was checked.
- Link each data set record to the models that used it, for example through the bill of materials (TEC-07).

Pitfalls:

- Assuming data found online is free to use for training.
- Recording provenance but not linking it to models, so the effect of a rights problem cannot be traced.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a model you train or tune, which data was used and where did each set come from?
- What rights do you hold over that data, and what limits apply to its use?
- If a source had to be withdrawn, could you identify every model that used it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Provenance records for training and test data sets
- Licence or rights documentation for externally sourced data
- Links between data sets and the models or versions that used them
- Preparation, labelling and synthetic data records

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Training and test data are gathered from wherever is convenient, and their origin is not recorded.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Origin is recorded for some data sets, but rights, licences and limits are not consistently checked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: For every data set used to train, tune or test AI, origin, rights, limits and preparation are recorded before use and linked to the models that used it.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Provenance records are checked for completeness before release, and when a source's rights or limits change, affected models are identified and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Provenance is captured automatically through data pipelines, and the approach is refined from audits, disputes and changes in rights or regulation.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Data provenance record template
- Data set to model link register

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Covers the technology through which AI is adopted: which tools and platforms people may use, how AI fits into the existing estate, where it is hosted, how models and prompts are tested, released and controlled, and how the organisation copes with fast change from suppliers. The aim is a small number of well understood routes that make the approved way the easy way.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation keeps a current list of approved AI tools and platforms, each with clear conditions of use, and staff know where to find it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A maintained list of approved AI tools and platforms exists.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each listed tool or platform, the list states its permitted uses, the data that may and may not be used with it, and its owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The list is published to all staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Staff have a route to request additions to the list.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The list covers the environments and toolchains used to build, test and run the organisation's own AI, each with an owner and support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Staff need a quick answer to which AI tools they can use and for what. An approved list with conditions turns policy into something people can act on, and gives procurement, security and data teams one place to record their decisions about each tool.

Reaching Level 3:

- List the AI tools and platforms already approved or in use, and confirm which are allowed.
- For each approved item, record permitted uses, data that may and may not be used with it, and an owner.
- Publish the list to all staff with a route to request additions.
- Where the organisation builds its own AI, add the environments and toolchains used to build, test and run it, each with an owner and support.

Pitfalls:

- Publishing a list without data rules, so staff know what tool to use but not what to put in it.
- Letting requests for additions sit unanswered, which pushes people to unapproved tools (TEC-08).

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Where would a member of staff look to find out which AI tools they may use, and for what data?
- How does a tool get added to or removed from the list, and how long does that take?
- When was the list last reviewed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The approved tools list with conditions of use, owners and review date
- The request process and a log of recent requests and decisions
- Approved build, test and run environments with owners

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No approved list; staff choose tools themselves or wait for case-by-case answers.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some tools are known to be allowed, but there is no maintained list, or conditions of use are missing or unclear.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A maintained, published list of approved AI tools and platforms states each one's permitted uses, data limits and owner, with a route to request additions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The list is reviewed on a set cycle, requests are handled within an agreed time, and use of approved tools is measured against the conditions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The list is refined from usage, requests and supplier change, and approval of new tools is quick enough that staff rarely look elsewhere.

parts.prose:
- Approved AI tools list
- Tool addition request form

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Agreed architecture patterns set out how AI components fit into the technology estate, and new uses of AI follow them or record why not. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Documented reference patterns with an owner cover the common ways AI is used in the estate.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The patterns are applied through design review, and departures are recorded and approved.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The patterns build in explainability and traceability of outputs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The degree of explainability each use of AI needs is set by its risk and audience.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The patterns build in input and output guardrails proportionate to risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Guardrails are re-evaluated when obligations or the risk assessment change.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Where the organisation builds or offers generative AI, the patterns mark its outputs as AI-generated in a machine-readable way.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without shared patterns each team solves the same problems differently, which raises cost and leaves an estate that is hard to support or secure. A small set of agreed patterns speeds delivery and makes AI services easier to run and change.

Reaching Level 3:

- Document reference patterns for the common ways AI is used in the estate, with an owner.
- Build into the patterns explainability and traceability of outputs, at a level set by risk and audience, and input and output guardrails proportionate to risk.
- Where the organisation builds or offers generative AI, include machine-readable marking of outputs as AI-generated.
- Apply the patterns through design review, recording and approving any departure.
- Re-evaluate guardrails when obligations or the risk assessment change.

Pitfalls:

- Writing patterns so abstract that design reviewers cannot tell whether a design follows them.
- Setting the same explainability level for every use regardless of risk.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Are there agreed patterns for how AI fits into your technology estate, and who owns them?
- How is a new use of AI checked against them at design stage?
- What happens when a team needs to depart from a pattern?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The reference architecture or pattern library for AI
- Design review records showing patterns applied or departures approved
- Output marking in generative AI patterns, where applicable

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No agreed patterns; each use of AI is designed from scratch.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some patterns or preferred approaches exist, but they are informal, partial or not used consistently.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Owned reference patterns cover the common uses of AI, are applied through design review, and build in explainability, traceability and guardrails proportionate to risk.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Conformance with the patterns is checked and reported, and departures are tracked to see whether they show a pattern needs to change.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Patterns are updated from delivery experience, operating data and technology change, and retired when better approaches arrive.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Reference pattern set
- Design review checklist
- Departure record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Requirements for where AI is hosted and where its data is processed and stored are defined, and each use of AI is checked against them before and during live use. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Documented requirements set where AI may be hosted and data processed for each class of data.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every use of AI is checked against the requirements before go-live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The pre go-live check covers subprocessors.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Many AI services process data in places the organisation has not chosen, sometimes in other jurisdictions or through subprocessors. Legal, contractual and sensitivity requirements on location only hold if they are stated and then checked against what the service actually does.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set requirements for where AI may be hosted and data processed, for each class of data, informed by legal obligations (RSK-04).
- Ask suppliers where they host and process data, and who their subprocessors are.
- Check every use of AI against the requirements before go-live, including subprocessors, and record the result.

Pitfalls:

- Checking the main supplier's location but not its subprocessors.
- Forgetting that a supplier can move processing after the contract is signed.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Where is each AI service hosted, and where is your data processed and stored, including by subprocessors?
- What are your requirements for location, and how are they set for different kinds of data?
- How would you find out if a supplier moved processing elsewhere?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Documented hosting and data location requirements
- Location checks for a sample of AI services, including subprocessor information

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Hosting and data location are not considered; they follow whatever the supplier offers.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Location is checked for some services, usually at purchase, without stated requirements or later checks.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Documented requirements set where AI may be hosted and data processed for each class of data, and every use, including subprocessors, is checked before go-live.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Compliance with location requirements is rechecked on a set cycle and when suppliers change terms or infrastructure, and breaches are acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Location requirements are refined from changes in law, risk and the market, and checks rely on continuous supplier attestation rather than one-off reviews.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Hosting and data location requirements
- Pre-go-live location check record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI is connected to core systems through supported, documented interfaces that the organisation can maintain, change and switch off. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every integration between AI and core systems uses supported interfaces.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each integration is documented with its owner and data flows.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each integration can be disabled without disrupting the core system.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The permissions and actions an AI system or agent holds on other systems are limited to what its purpose needs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Those permissions and actions are approved and risk assessed.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI is most useful when it works with the systems people already use, but informal connections break silently, are hard to change and can become critical without anyone noticing. Supported and documented integration keeps AI services maintainable and lets them be removed cleanly.

Reaching Level 3:

- Require every integration between AI and core systems to use supported interfaces.
- Document each integration with its owner and data flows.
- Design and test a way to disable each integration without disrupting the core system.
- Limit the permissions and actions each AI system or agent holds on other systems to what its purpose needs, and get them approved and risk assessed.

Pitfalls:

- Giving an agent write access to a core system when read access would do.
- Never testing the switch-off, so nobody knows whether it works.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How is this AI service connected to the systems it reads from and writes to?
- Where are those integrations documented, and who supports them?
- If you had to switch the AI service off tomorrow, what would break?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Integration documentation showing interfaces, data flows and owners
- Support arrangements for AI integrations
- Permission and action limits for AI systems and agents, with approvals and risk assessments

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI is connected to other systems by whatever means works, often manual workarounds or unsupported links.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some integrations are documented and supported, but others are informal or known only to the people who built them.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every integration between AI and core systems is supported, documented and can be switched off safely, and AI permissions on other systems are limited and approved.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Integration health and failures are tracked, undocumented integrations are found and brought under control, and changes go through managed change.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Integration patterns are standardised and reused, and improved from incidents and change experience.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Integration register with owners and data flows
- Permission approval record for AI systems and agents

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Models, prompts and their configuration are versioned and released under control, so the organisation knows what is running and can roll back to a known good version. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Models, prompts and configuration are under version control.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Data sets used with each model are versioned alongside each model version.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Changes are released through a controlled process with approval.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every live use of AI can be rolled back to a previous known good version.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Documentation is kept for each version, suited to its users, operators and, where relevant, regulators, stating intended purpose and users, how it works, inputs and outputs, known limitations, and where it must not be used or relied on.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Release approval includes checking the documentation against the released version.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Users are told in advance, accessibly, of planned changes that affect them.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A small change to a model, prompt or setting can change behaviour as much as a code change, and suppliers may change models without notice. Version and release control means problems can be traced to a change and reversed quickly.

Reaching Level 3:

- Version models, prompts, configuration and the data sets used with each model version.
- Release changes through a controlled process with approval, and keep the previous known good version ready for rollback.
- Keep documentation for each version suited to users, operators and, where relevant, regulators, covering intended purpose and users, how it works, inputs and outputs, known limits and where it must not be used or relied on.
- Check the documentation against the released version as part of release approval.
- Tell affected users in advance, accessibly, about planned changes.

Pitfalls:

- Not tracking which version of a supplier's model is behind a service.
- Letting documentation drift from what is actually running.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which version of the model, prompts and configuration is running in live use right now?
- How is a change released, and who approves it?
- When did you last roll back, and how long did it take?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Version history for models, prompts and configuration
- Release records with approvals
- A record of a rollback or rollback test
- Documentation for the current version, written for users, operators and regulators
- Use documentation stating purpose, users, limitations and where not to rely on it; advance notices of changes

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Models and prompts are changed directly in live use; there is no record of what changed or when.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some versioning exists, for example for in-house models, but prompts, settings or supplier model versions are not controlled and rollback is uncertain.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Models, prompts and configuration are versioned, released with approval and can be rolled back, with documentation for each version and advance notice of changes to users.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Releases and rollbacks are recorded and reviewed, unplanned changes including supplier model updates are detected, and failed releases are investigated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Release and rollback are largely automated and routinely exercised, and the process is refined from release outcomes.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Version register for models, prompts and data sets
- Release approval record
- Per-version documentation template
- Rollback procedure

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before release, each AI system is tested for accuracy, robustness and behaviour against acceptance criteria agreed in advance, and released only if it meets them. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Acceptance criteria for accuracy, robustness and behaviour are agreed before testing starts.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Intended operating conditions (where, when and on what inputs the AI can be relied on) are defined before testing and given to operators and risk owners.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Limits on the system keep its use within the intended operating conditions.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Testing uses representative data, including edge cases, kept independent of any data used to train or tune the model.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Testing of generative AI covers harmful output.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Testing checks the explainability achieved against what was required and records its limits.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Test results are recorded and signed off before every release.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The testing approach and its metrics are reviewed on a set cycle against live performance and incidents.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI can perform well in a demonstration and badly on real cases, unusual inputs or the groups it serves least well. Testing against criteria set before results are seen gives the release decision an objective basis and a record to compare live performance with.

Reaching Level 3:

- Before testing, define the intended operating conditions and agree acceptance criteria for accuracy, robustness, behaviour and explainability, taken from the measures in MON-01.
- Test with representative data, including edge cases, kept independent of training data, and for generative AI include harmful output; security testing is SEC-06.
- Record and sign off results before every release, give operators and risk owners the operating conditions, and enforce them with limits.
- Review the testing approach and metrics on a fixed cycle against live performance and incidents.

Pitfalls:

- Setting acceptance criteria after seeing the results.
- Testing on data that overlaps the training data, which flatters accuracy.
- Describing operating conditions to operators but not enforcing them in the system.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What criteria must this system meet before it is released, and when were they agreed?
- Does the test data reflect the real cases and people the system will meet, including unusual ones?
- Who signs off test results, and what happens when a criterion is missed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Acceptance criteria and test plans for a sample of releases
- Test results and release sign-off records
- Review records for the testing approach, and harmful output tests for generative AI
- Defined operating conditions and their enforcement

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Systems are tried informally before release; there are no acceptance criteria.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some testing is done, but criteria are set after the fact, test data is unrepresentative, or robustness and behaviour are not covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every release is tested against criteria and operating conditions set in advance, on representative data, with results signed off and the approach reviewed against live performance.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Test coverage and results are reviewed across uses, releases that miss criteria are blocked or formally accepted, and test results are compared with live performance.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Test methods and criteria are refined from live performance and incidents, and evaluation is automated and repeated for every change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Test plan with acceptance criteria
- Operating conditions statement
- Test results and sign-off record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation plans for changes to models, suppliers and platforms, including suppliers withdrawing models, so that AI services continue without disruption. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every AI service has a maintained bill of materials covering its models, data sets, libraries, services, suppliers and platforms, with their known end dates.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each AI service has a refresh plan with an owner and a budget for planned change.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Concentration on a single foundation model or supplier is recorded as a dependency risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each bill of materials is reviewed on a set cycle and on significant change.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI models and platforms are replaced and withdrawn far faster than most enterprise technology, often on the supplier's timetable. Planning for that change avoids services stopping or being kept on unsupported versions, and keeps the organisation able to move to better options.

Reaching Level 3:

- Build a bill of materials for every AI service, listing models, data sets, libraries, services, suppliers and platforms with known end dates.
- Give each service a refresh plan, owner and budget for planned change.
- Record reliance on a single foundation model or supplier as a dependency risk.
- Review each bill of materials on a fixed cycle and whenever there is significant change.

Pitfalls:

- Learning of a model's withdrawal from the supplier's notice instead of a tracked end date.
- Planning refreshes with no budget set aside.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which models, suppliers and platforms does each AI service depend on, and when might they change or be withdrawn?
- How would you learn that a supplier was retiring a model you rely on?
- What would it take to move a service to a different model or platform?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Bill of materials for each AI service with its last review date
- A dependency record showing models, platforms, versions and known end dates
- Refresh plans and budget lines for planned change
- Dependency records showing concentration on single models or suppliers

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Change is handled when it is forced; supplier withdrawals arrive as surprises.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some services track supplier roadmaps or end-of-life dates, but there is no consistent planning or capacity for change.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every AI service has a maintained, regularly reviewed bill of materials with end dates, a funded refresh plan, and recorded concentration risk.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Dependency end dates and supplier notices are tracked across the estate, changes are scheduled ahead of deadlines, and services caught by unplanned change are reviewed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Services are designed so models and platforms can be swapped with little rework, and refresh planning is improved from experience of past changes.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Bill of materials per AI service
- Refresh plan

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Use of unapproved AI tools is detected, and people using them are steered to an approved alternative or a route to get their need met. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Defined means detect use of unapproved AI tools across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each finding of unapproved use is recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each finding leads to the person being steered to an approved tool or a request route.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
When approved options are slow or missing, people use whatever is to hand, often with organisational data. Finding that use, and responding by meeting the need rather than only blocking it, reduces the risk and shows where the approved list falls short.

Reaching Level 3:

- Decide the means of detecting unapproved AI tool use, such as network or browser logs, expense claims and staff surveys, and apply them across the organisation.
- Respond to each finding by steering the person to an approved tool from TEC-01 or to the request route.
- Record each finding and the response, and pass compliance matters to GOV-08.

Pitfalls:

- Responding only by blocking, which drives use to personal devices.
- Treating findings as disciplinary matters when the need behind them is unmet.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you find out which AI tools people use that are not approved?
- When you find one in use, what happens to the person and to the need behind it?
- Is unapproved use going up or down, and how do you know?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Detection reports or records of unapproved AI tool use
- Records of responses, including tools added to the approved list as a result

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No one knows which unapproved AI tools are in use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some unapproved use is known about, through reports or occasional checks, but responses are inconsistent or limited to blocking.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Unapproved AI tool use is detected by defined means across the organisation, and each finding is recorded and leads to the person being steered to an approved route.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The level of unapproved use is measured over time, repeat or high-risk use is escalated, and findings feed changes to the approved tools list.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Unapproved use is low because approved options meet need, and detection and response are refined from trends and new kinds of tool.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Detection method description
- Unapproved tool findings log

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Sets out what an organisation needs in place to adopt AI securely. This is a bridge domain: it asks whether the organisation has adopted a security baseline for AI, assesses AI-specific threats, manages the security of its AI supply chain, protects information, tests AI security before release and can respond to AI security incidents. The detailed technical controls are delegated to recognised AI security frameworks, which the baseline in SEC-01 is expected to draw on. Keeping services running when AI fails or gets things wrong is OPM-09.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation has adopted a recognised AI security baseline, built it into its security standards, and applies it to every use of AI. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A recognised AI security baseline is adopted and has an owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline is written into the organisation's security standards.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline is applied to every use of AI before it goes live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every live use of AI is within security monitoring.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Logs for each use of AI support detecting and investigating AI-specific attacks, at a depth set by risk.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
General security standards were not written with AI in mind and miss threats specific to models, prompts and training data. Adopting a recognised baseline saves the organisation inventing its own and gives assessors, suppliers and staff a shared reference point.

Reaching Level 3:

- Choose a recognised AI security control set as the baseline and name its owner.
- Write the baseline into the organisation's security standards.
- Apply the baseline to every use of AI before it goes live and record the result.
- Bring every live use of AI into security monitoring, with logs deep enough, by risk, to detect and investigate AI-specific attacks.

Pitfalls:

- Writing a new baseline from scratch instead of adopting one that already exists.
- Applying the baseline to new uses but not to AI already in use.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which AI security baseline has the organisation adopted, and who owns it?
- How is the baseline applied to a new use of AI, including AI inside bought products?
- How do you know which uses of AI meet the baseline and which do not?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The adopted baseline and the security standard or policy that references it
- Conformance records for a sample of uses of AI
- A register of baseline gaps with owners and risk acceptance decisions
- Security monitoring coverage for live uses of AI, with AI-relevant log sources

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No AI security baseline; security reviews of AI depend on the knowledge of whichever specialist is asked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A baseline has been chosen or drafted, but it is applied only to some uses of AI or is not yet part of security standards.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An owned, recognised AI security baseline is part of security standards and applied before go-live, and every live use is monitored with logs set by risk.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Conformance with the baseline is checked and reported for each use of AI, and gaps are tracked to closure or formally accepted.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The baseline is updated from incidents, threat intelligence and changes in recognised frameworks, and the organisation contributes to shared practice.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Baseline adoption decision
- Baseline compliance record per use
- Monitoring and logging coverage list

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each use of AI has its AI-specific threats assessed before it goes live and again when it changes, and the results shape its design and controls. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined threat modelling approach covers AI-specific threats.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Threat modelling is required for every use of AI, proportionate to risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Threats assessed include impersonation of the organisation or its people through synthetic media.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Threat modelling findings are recorded for each use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Threat modelling findings are acted on.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Threat modelling for agents covers instructions hidden in content they read, misuse of their tools, and chains of actions that go beyond their purpose.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI introduces ways of attacking a service that conventional threat assessment does not look for, such as manipulated inputs, poisoned training data and misuse of connected tools. Assessing these per use, in proportion to risk, finds problems while they are still cheap to fix.

Reaching Level 3:

- Adopt a threat modelling approach that covers AI-specific threats, such as manipulated inputs, poisoned training data and impersonation through synthetic media.
- Require a threat model for every use of AI, scaled to its risk (RSK-02), before go-live and when it changes.
- Record findings and track the resulting actions to completion.

Pitfalls:

- Using a conventional method that misses threats unique to AI.
- Producing a threat model that nobody acts on.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is threat modelling required for every use of AI, and does it cover threats specific to AI?
- Who carries it out, and do they have the AI knowledge to do it well?
- Show how the findings of a recent threat model changed the design or controls.

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Agent threat models covering hidden instructions and tool misuse
- The threat modelling method or guidance, showing AI-specific threats
- Completed threat models for a sample of uses, with findings and actions
- Synthetic media impersonation covered in threat models

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI-specific threats are considered only when an individual raises them.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Threat modelling covers AI for some uses or teams, or uses conventional methods that miss AI-specific threats.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A defined approach covering AI-specific threats, including synthetic media impersonation, is required for every use of AI, with findings recorded and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Threat models are reviewed when uses change or new threats emerge, completion is measured, and untreated findings are escalated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Threat modelling is refined from incidents, testing results and external threat intelligence, and common threats are handled once in shared patterns.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI threat modelling guide
- Threat model template
- Findings and actions log

controls.title: Security of the AI supply chain

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The security of models, data, code and services obtained from others is assessed before use and managed for as long as they are in use. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined process assesses the security of every external model, data set and component before use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The source of each external model, data set and component is recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Security expectations are set for suppliers.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For each AI service obtained from others, the split of security responsibilities with the provider is documented and reviewed on significant change and at set intervals.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The organisation's share of those security responsibilities is implemented and checked.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Organisations that receive AI from this organisation are told which security responsibilities they hold.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: External models and components are reassessed at set intervals and when vulnerabilities are disclosed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Disclosed vulnerabilities in external models and components are tracked to mitigation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Most organisations will use models, datasets and components they did not create, and a weakness in any of them becomes a weakness in the service. Knowing where each component came from and holding suppliers to security expectations is the only way to manage a risk the organisation does not directly control.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define a process to assess the security of every external model, dataset and component before use, including freely downloaded ones, and record its source.
- Set security expectations for suppliers, feeding the contract terms in OPM-04.
- For each AI service from others, document the split of security responsibilities, implement and check the organisation's share, and review the split at set intervals and on significant change.
- Where the organisation provides AI to others, tell them which security responsibilities they hold.
- Reassess external models and components at set intervals and when vulnerabilities are disclosed, tracking each to mitigation.

Pitfalls:

- Checking purchased products but not open models downloaded by developers.
- Assuming the provider handles all security for a hosted service.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you check the security of a model, dataset or component before it is used?
- Does that check apply to freely downloaded models and to AI inside bought products?
- What happens when a supplier changes a model or a weakness is found in a component?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Responsibility split for each AI service obtained from others, with checks of the organisation's share and review dates
- The supply chain security assessment process and a sample of completed assessments
- A record of external AI components in use, with source and version
- Security clauses or schedules in AI supplier contracts

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Models, data and components are taken from suppliers or public sources without a security check.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some security checks happen, usually for large procurements, but freely available models and components are not covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: External models, data and components are security assessed before use and reassessed over time, with security responsibilities split, documented and checked for each service from others.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Supplier security and reassessment results are measured and reported, and overdue reassessments or unmitigated vulnerabilities are escalated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Supply chain assurance is improved from incidents and supplier performance, and the organisation shares findings with peers and suppliers.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- External component assessment record
- Shared responsibility matrix per service
- Vulnerability tracking log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Sensitive information is protected from exposure through AI tools, prompts, training and outputs, with rules staff understand and technical measures that enforce them. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Rules set out which classes of information may be used with which AI tools.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The rules are communicated to all staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Technical measures on approved tools support the rules.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Models trained or tuned on protected information are handled at least at that protection level, taking account of aggregation.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI tools make it easy to paste sensitive material into a service that stores or learns from it, and outputs can reveal information the user was never entitled to see. Clear rules backed by technical measures protect information without forcing people away from approved tools.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set rules for which classes of information may be used with which AI tools, linked to the approved tools list (TEC-01).
- Tell all staff the rules and include them in AI literacy learning (PPL-01).
- Configure technical measures on approved tools to enforce the rules, such as data loss prevention and supplier settings that stop retention or training on inputs.
- Handle any model trained or tuned on protected information at least at that protection level, taking account of what combined data could reveal.

Pitfalls:

- Relying on guidance alone with no technical measures behind it.
- Forgetting that a model can expose its training data through its outputs.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which classes of information may be used with which AI tools, and how do staff know?
- What stops sensitive information leaking through prompts, stored conversations or outputs?
- How would you know if sensitive information had been put into an AI tool it should not have been?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Rules or guidance linking information classification to AI tools
- Configuration or monitoring records for leakage prevention on approved tools
- Protection level records for models trained or tuned on protected information

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No specific rules; staff decide for themselves what information to put into AI tools.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Guidance exists on what not to share with AI tools, but it is not enforced and does not cover outputs or training.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Rules on which information may be used with which AI tools are communicated to staff and backed by technical measures, and tuned models inherit their data's protection.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Leakage controls are monitored, attempted exposures are detected and followed up, and results are reported.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Controls are refined from monitoring and incident data so that protection improves without adding friction for legitimate use.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Information and AI tool use rules
- Technical control settings record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Security incident management covers incidents involving AI, with playbooks, people who have the skills to handle them, and the ability to contain an affected AI service quickly. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Security incident procedures include AI-specific scenarios, each with a playbook.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Playbooks cover recovery from AI-specific attacks to a known good state, linked to continuity plans, and support for affected users and other parties.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each AI service has a known way to contain it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Responders are trained for the AI-specific scenarios.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: AI scenarios are exercised on a set cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Agreements with those the organisation provides AI to set out the incident support they and affected users will receive.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A published vulnerability disclosure route covers the organisation's AI services, and reports feed incident handling.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Notification routes and deadlines for security breaches, including breaches in the AI supply chain, to regulators, customers and affected parties are set out as law and agreements require.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
An attack on or through an AI service can look different from a conventional incident and may need a model, tool or integration to be switched off fast. Preparing before an incident happens avoids slow, improvised responses. Non-security AI incidents are handled under MON-04.

Reaching Level 3:

- Add AI-specific scenarios and playbooks to security incident procedures, including how to contain each AI service and recover it to a known good state, linked to continuity plans (OPM-09).
- Include support for affected users and other parties in the playbooks, and set it out in agreements where the organisation provides AI to others.
- Train responders for the AI scenarios and exercise them on a fixed cycle.
- Publish a vulnerability disclosure route covering AI services and feed reports into incident handling.
- Set out notification routes and deadlines for security breaches, including in the AI supply chain, to regulators, customers and affected parties as law and agreements require.

Pitfalls:

- Having no quick way to switch off a compromised AI service.
- Treating AI incidents as general IT incidents, so responders miss what makes them different.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Does the security incident process cover incidents involving AI, and with what playbooks?
- Who would respond to an AI security incident, and have they been trained or exercised for it?
- How quickly could you contain or switch off an affected AI service?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Incident procedures and playbooks covering AI scenarios
- Records of exercises or real incidents involving AI, with lessons and actions
- Recovery playbooks, the published vulnerability disclosure route and exercise records

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Response performance is measured, and lessons from exercises and real incidents are acted on.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Incident response for AI is improved from exercise results, real incidents and external threat information, and lessons are shared with peers.

controls.title: Security testing of AI before release

links.text: Control page on the AACF website

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before release, each AI system is security tested against the threats in its threat model by suitably skilled testers, including checks that it does not disclose personal or sensitive information. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Security testing before release covers the threats in the use's threat model.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Security testing is carried out by testers with the right skills.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: For higher-risk uses, security testers are independent of the build team.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Testing of generative AI includes attempts to bypass its safeguards.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Testing checks that personal or sensitive information is not disclosed through the system.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Before release, testing tries to make each agent act outside its approved permissions, including through instructions hidden in content it reads.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
An AI system that passes its accuracy tests can still be manipulated, talked out of its safeguards or made to reveal information it holds. Testing against the threats found for the use, by people who know how AI is attacked, finds these weaknesses before an attacker does.

Reaching Level 3:

- Plan security testing for each release from the use's threat model (SEC-02), so every identified threat is tested.
- Use testers with the right skills for AI, and for higher-risk uses testers who are independent of the build team.
- For generative AI, include attempts to bypass safeguards, and for every use check that personal or sensitive information is not disclosed through the system.
- Record the results alongside the other test results so they inform the release sign-off (TEC-06).

Pitfalls:

- Running conventional security tests that miss threats unique to AI.
- Letting the build team mark its own security testing on a higher-risk use.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Does security testing before release cover the threats in the use's threat model?
- Who carries out the security testing, what AI skills do they have, and are they independent of the build team for higher-risk uses?
- How do you test that safeguards cannot be bypassed and that personal or sensitive information is not disclosed?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Test records of attempts to make agents act outside their permissions
- Security test plans and results for a sample of releases, traced to the threat model
- Tester skills and independence records for higher-risk uses
- Safeguard bypass test results for generative AI
- Information disclosure test results

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Systems are released without security testing, or with conventional checks that miss AI-specific threats.

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Some security testing is done, but it is not driven by the threat model, testers lack AI skills, or safeguard bypass and information disclosure are not covered.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every release is security tested against its threat model by suitably skilled testers, independent for higher-risk uses, including safeguard bypass for generative AI and checks for disclosure of personal or sensitive information.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Security test coverage and findings are reviewed across uses, and releases with unresolved findings are blocked or formally accepted.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Security test methods are refined from incidents and live performance, and security testing is repeated for every change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Security test plan traced to the threat model
- Security test results record

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Covers the knowledge and skills people need to use AI safely and well, from a baseline for everyone to specialist careers, and how the organisation plans for the effect of AI on its workforce. Capability should be built inside the organisation rather than rented, and changes to roles should be planned in the open with the people affected.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Everyone in the organisation has a baseline understanding of what AI is, what it can and cannot do, and how to use it safely under the organisation's policy. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined AI literacy baseline covers what AI can do, its limits and its risks.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline covers the AI policy, the adopted ethical principles, and the environmental and social impact of AI use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline covers the AI security threats relevant to all staff, and updates are issued as new threats appear.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline is required for all staff, including new joiners.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The baseline is also required for contractors and others who operate AI on the organisation's behalf.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Completion of the baseline is recorded for everyone it is required of.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Staff meet AI in the tools they already use, whether or not the organisation plans for it. A shared baseline lets people spot unreliable output, avoid sharing what they should not, and see where AI could help their work.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a short literacy baseline that covers what AI can and cannot do, its main risks, the security threats every member of staff could meet, the AI policy (GOV-01), the adopted ethical principles (RSK-05) and the environmental and social effects of AI use.
- Name an owner for the baseline and set a way to send staff brief updates when a new threat or significant tool change appears.
- Make the baseline required for all staff, add it to the joining process, and make it a condition for contractors and others who operate AI on your behalf.
- Record completion for every group, including contractors, in one place that can be reported by team.

Pitfalls:

- Teaching only how to use one tool, so staff learn the buttons but not the limits and risks.
- Leaving contractors and temporary staff out because they sit outside the normal learning system.
- Writing the security content once and never updating it as new threats appear.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What does every member of staff need to know about AI, and where is that set out?
- How many staff have completed it, including new joiners and contractors?
- How do you know people understand it, not just that they completed it?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The literacy baseline or curriculum, with an owner and review date
- Completion records by group
- Results of knowledge checks or surveys
- Literacy completion records for contractors who operate AI
- AI security content in the literacy baseline and recent threat updates

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No organisation-wide AI learning; understanding depends on individual interest.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some AI awareness material exists, but it is optional, reaches few staff or is out of date.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Everyone who uses or operates AI for the organisation must complete a defined AI literacy baseline that is kept current, and completion is recorded.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Completion and understanding are measured across the organisation, gaps by group are followed up, and content is refreshed on a set cycle.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The baseline is updated from incidents, staff feedback and changes in AI tools, and its effect on safe use is assessed.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI literacy baseline with owner and review date
- Completion register covering staff and contractors
- Threat update bulletin template

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Leaders understand AI well enough to set direction for it, question proposals and risks, and make informed decisions about its use. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined leadership learning offer covers AI opportunity, risk, governance and the questions leaders should ask.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Board members, executives and senior managers have completed the offer.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Leaders approve AI investment, accept its risks and set the tone for how staff use it. If they cannot judge claims made for AI, decisions are left to enthusiasts or vendors, or are not taken at all.

Reaching Level 3:

- Agree what the board, executive and senior managers need to understand about AI opportunity, risk, governance and the questions to ask of a proposal.
- Build or buy a short leadership session or series that covers those four topics, using examples from your own organisation where possible.
- Schedule it so every board member, executive and senior manager completes it, including new appointees.
- Record attendance and give leaders a one-page list of challenge questions to use at decision points (GOV-03, POR-04).

Pitfalls:

- Relying on vendor briefings, which explain the product's benefits rather than how to judge them.
- Covering opportunity only and leaving out risk and governance.
- Letting the board opt out because members are assumed to know enough already.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What are leaders expected to understand about AI, and how was that decided?
- Which members of the board and executive have completed AI learning?
- Give an example of a leader challenging an AI proposal or risk.

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The leadership learning offer and attendance records
- Board or committee minutes showing informed challenge on AI

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Leaders' understanding of AI depends on personal interest and vendor briefings.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some leaders have attended AI briefings, but there is no defined expectation of what leaders should know.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Board members, executives and senior managers have completed a defined learning offer on AI opportunity, risk and governance.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Leadership capability is assessed, gaps are addressed, and the quality of AI decisions and challenge is reviewed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Leadership learning is updated from decision reviews and external change, and leaders keep their knowledge current through ongoing exposure to AI in practice.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation defines the specialist AI roles it needs, with career paths and a professional community that help people grow and stay. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Specialist AI roles are defined and the same definitions are used across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each specialist AI role has stated skills expectations.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Career paths are set out for specialist AI roles.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A professional community for AI specialists is in place and active.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Specialists who have no defined role or route to progress tend to leave or move into unrelated work. Clear roles and careers make it possible to recruit, develop and keep the people who build, assure and run AI.

Reaching Level 3:

- List the specialist AI roles the organisation needs, using the skills assessment (PPL-04) as the starting point.
- Write one role profile per specialist role with skills expectations, and agree common titles and grades across the organisation.
- Set out a career path for each role family showing how people progress and what they need to show at each step.
- Set up a professional community for specialists with a named lead, regular meetings and a shared space, and keep a record of its activity.

Pitfalls:

- Letting each team invent its own titles and grades, which blocks movement and fair pay.
- Defining roles without a route upwards, so experienced specialists leave to progress.
- Starting a community with no lead or time set aside, so it fades after a few meetings.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which specialist AI roles does the organisation need, and are they defined?
- How does a specialist progress, and what professional community can they join?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Role profiles and career framework for AI specialists
- Professional community terms of reference or activity records

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Specialist AI work is done by people in unrelated roles with no recognition or route to progress.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some AI roles are defined locally, but titles, grades and expectations differ across the organisation.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Specialist AI roles are defined in the same way across the organisation, with skills expectations, career paths and an active professional community.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progression, retention and role coverage for specialists are measured and reported, and gaps or attrition are acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Roles and career paths are updated as AI work changes, and the organisation is known as a place where specialists develop.

parts.prose:
- Specialist AI role profiles
- AI career framework
- Professional community terms of reference
