parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation knows which AI skills it has and which it needs, by role and group, and uses this to plan learning, recruitment and workforce decisions. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI skills each role needs are defined.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Current AI skills have been assessed across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The gap between needed and current skills is recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Learning and recruitment plans are based on the recorded gap.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Learning and recruitment spent without knowing the gap is often wasted. A skills assessment shows where capability is missing and gives a baseline to measure progress against.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define the AI skills each role or role group needs, starting with the roles that use, build, buy or assure AI most.
- Assess current skills across the whole organisation using a simple self-assessment checked by managers, or a short skills test for specialist roles.
- Record the gap by role and group in a single register.
- Use the gap to set learning priorities (PPL-05) and recruitment needs (PPL-07), and record which actions came from it.

Pitfalls:

- Assessing only the technology team and missing the skills needed by everyone else who works with AI.
- Running a survey and filing the results without changing any plan.
- Using a skills list so long that people cannot assess themselves against it honestly.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What AI skills does each role or group need, and how was that worked out?
- When were current skills last assessed, and what did it show?
- How have the results changed learning or recruitment plans?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- A skills framework or needs analysis for AI by role
- Skills assessment results and the resulting plan

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No assessment; skills are known only through individual managers' impressions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Skills have been assessed once, or only for some groups, and the results are not used to plan.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: The AI skills each role needs are defined, current skills are assessed across the organisation, and the recorded gap drives learning and recruitment plans.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Skills are reassessed on a set cycle, progress against the gap is measured, and priority gaps are tracked to closure.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Skills needs are anticipated from the AI roadmap and external change, and the assessment method is improved from experience.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI skills framework by role
- Skills assessment questionnaire
- Skills gap register with resulting actions

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: People can get learning matched to what their role needs to do with AI, beyond the baseline for all staff, and use it in their work. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Learning pathways are defined for each role group that works with AI and are linked to the skills assessment.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The pathways are resourced and available across the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The pathways cover the specific risk management duties of each role group.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The pathways extend to suppliers and contractors who operate AI for the organisation.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Pathways for roles that build, run, buy or secure AI include AI security.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Pathways for people who build AI include secure design and development.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI security content of pathways is reviewed when significant new threats emerge.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
What a caseworker, a developer, a procurement officer and an auditor need to know about AI differs. Learning built around roles is more likely to change how people work than generic courses.

Reaching Level 3:

- Identify the role groups that work with AI and, for each, write a learning pathway built from the gaps found in the skills assessment (PPL-04).
- Include in each pathway the risk management duties that role holds, and add AI security for roles that build, run, buy or secure AI, with secure design and development for builders.
- Fund the pathways, make them available across the organisation, and require suppliers and contractors who operate AI for you to follow the relevant pathway.
- Set a trigger to review security content when a significant new threat emerges, and name who carries out that review.

Pitfalls:

- Offering a generic catalogue of courses that no one has linked to actual role needs.
- Forgetting that buyers and risk staff need AI learning as much as developers do.
- Assuming suppliers already know your risk duties and security rules.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What learning is available for roles that build, buy, assure or use AI heavily?
- How does it link to the skills gaps you have identified?
- How do you know it has changed how people work?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Role-based learning pathways and the needs they address
- Uptake records and evaluation results
- Learning records for people with AI risk duties, including contractors
- AI security in learning pathways for builders, operators, buyers and security staff

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Learning beyond the baseline depends on individuals finding their own courses.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some role-specific learning exists, but coverage is uneven and not linked to assessed needs.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Resourced learning pathways, linked to the skills assessment, exist for every role group that works with AI, including suppliers, and cover risk duties and AI security.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Uptake and the effect of learning on work are measured, and pathways with low uptake or effect are changed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Pathways are updated from skills reassessment, feedback and changes in AI tools, and include learning on the job as well as formal courses.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Role-based learning pathway map
- Learning records for people with AI risk duties
- Security content review trigger log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills is planned for openly, with affected staff and their representatives informed and involved, and decisions made fairly. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Workforce plans include the expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The plans set out options for affected staff, such as reskilling and redeployment.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The plans are shared with staff and their representatives.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI can change what roles involve, create new ones and reduce demand for some tasks. Planning this in the open, and treating redeployment, reskilling and growth as real options, keeps trust and avoids losing knowledge the organisation still needs.

Reaching Level 3:

- Add a section to the workforce plan that sets out the expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills, drawing on the AI use boundaries (STR-02) and the skills gap (PPL-04).
- Set out the options for affected staff, such as reskilling, redeployment and new roles, and how choices between them will be made fairly.
- Share the plan with staff and their representatives before decisions are taken, and record when and how this was done.
- Name an owner to update the plan as new uses of AI are approved.

Pitfalls:

- Keeping the workforce effect confidential until changes are already decided, which destroys trust.
- Treating headcount reduction as the only outcome and not planning reskilling or redeployment.
- Planning one project at a time with no view across the organisation.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How does workforce planning account for the effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills?
- When and how are affected staff and their representatives told and involved?
- What options are offered to people whose roles change, and how are outcomes checked for fairness?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Workforce plans showing the expected effect of AI
- Records of consultation or engagement with staff and representatives
- Reskilling or redeployment records and outcome monitoring

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: The effect of AI on the workforce is not considered until changes are already under way.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Effects are considered for individual projects, but there is no organisation-wide view and staff learn of changes late.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Workforce plans set out the expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills, with options for affected staff, and are shared with staff and representatives.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Actual effects on roles and skills are tracked against the plan, fairness of outcomes across groups is checked, and differences are acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Workforce planning for AI is updated from outcomes and external change, and staff help shape how roles develop.

parts.prose:
- AI section of the workforce plan
- Reskilling and redeployment options paper
- Record of sharing with staff and representatives

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation recruits and keeps the AI expertise it needs and uses external experts in a way that transfers knowledge, so that capability stays when contracts end. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A plan for recruiting and retaining AI expertise is in place.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The plan addresses the diversity of AI teams.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each external engagement for AI expertise includes defined knowledge transfer to named internal staff.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Demand for AI expertise is high and organisations often rely on contractors and suppliers. Without deliberate knowledge transfer, each engagement leaves the organisation no more capable than before and dependent on the next one.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a short plan for recruiting and retaining AI expertise, covering where to find candidates, what keeps them, and how you will build diversity in AI teams.
- Add a standard knowledge transfer clause to contracts with AI suppliers and contractors that names what must be handed over and how.
- Name the internal staff who will receive the knowledge in each external engagement before it starts.
- Keep a list of engagements with their named recipients so gaps can be seen.

Pitfalls:

- Naming no internal recipient, so knowledge transfer becomes a document nobody reads.
- Treating diversity as a recruitment statistic only, with no action in the plan.
- Renewing the same contractor year after year without asking why the skill was never built inside.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you attract and keep people with AI expertise?
- When you use contractors or suppliers for AI, how is their knowledge passed to your own staff?
- Which AI capabilities would be lost if a key contract or person left tomorrow?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Recruitment and retention plan or data for AI roles
- Knowledge transfer clauses or records from external engagements

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Expertise is hired or contracted as needs arise, with no plan for keeping knowledge.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Recruitment for AI roles happens, but retention is not managed and external engagements rarely include knowledge transfer.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A plan covers recruiting, retaining and diversifying AI expertise, and every external engagement transfers knowledge to named internal staff.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Time to hire, retention and reliance on external expertise are measured, and knowledge transfer is checked at the end of each engagement.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The balance of internal and external expertise is set deliberately from evidence and adjusted as needs change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI recruitment and retention plan
- Knowledge transfer contract clause
- Engagement register with named internal recipients

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: People using AI day to day can get practical help, current guidance and answers to their questions quickly from a known place. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A known support route offers guidance, examples and answers for every approved AI tool.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The support route is resourced.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Guidance is updated when approved tools change.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Guidance for each approved tool states its known limitations, failure modes and residual security risks, and what users should do about them.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Users are told promptly of changes to approved tools that affect security.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Training fades and tools change. People who cannot get help when they are stuck either stop using AI or find their own ways round problems, which is where mistakes and unsafe use start.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set up one known support route for all approved AI tools (TEC-01), such as an intranet page with a question channel, and give it named people with time to run it.
- Write guidance for each approved tool with examples, known limitations, failure modes and residual security risks, and what users should do about each.
- Agree a routine with the owners of each tool so guidance is updated whenever the tool changes.
- Set up a way to tell users promptly about security-relevant changes, such as a short notice on the support page and a message to users.

Pitfalls:

- Relying on a champions network (CUL-06) alone, which is a peer network and not a resourced support route.
- Publishing guidance at launch and never updating it when the tool changes.
- Describing only what a tool can do and leaving out where it fails.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Where does someone go when they are unsure how to use an AI tool safely or well?
- Who keeps the guidance current when tools change?
- What are the most common questions, and what has changed as a result?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The support route and guidance, with update dates
- Support request data or logs showing common themes and actions
- Tool guidance stating limitations, failure modes and residual risks

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Help depends on knowing someone who understands the tool.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some guidance or a help channel exists for particular tools or teams, but it is hard to find or not kept current.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A known, resourced support route gives current guidance on every approved AI tool, including its limits and security risks, and tells users promptly of security changes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Use of support, common questions and response times are measured, and recurring problems feed changes to guidance, learning or tools.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Support is shaped by how people actually use AI, and good practice from users is captured and shared back.

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Covers the human side of adopting AI: managing it as organisational change, telling people plainly what is happening and why, involving staff and their representatives, making it safe to raise problems, and keeping the trust of the people the organisation serves. Technology that people do not trust or understand is either not used or used badly, so these controls decide whether the rest of the framework produces real benefit.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI adoption is managed as organisational change, with a change plan, named sponsors and the resources to carry it out. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An assessment of the current culture and what has to change for AI adoption has been carried out.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A documented change plan for AI adoption is in place and builds on that assessment.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The change plan has named senior sponsors.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A funded change resource is in place to carry out the plan.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The change plan is applied to every significant use of AI.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Most of the effort in adopting AI goes into changing how people work, not into the technology. Treating adoption as a technology rollout leaves processes, roles and habits unchanged, and the expected benefits do not arrive.

Reaching Level 3:

- Assess the current culture and how people work today, using a short survey and conversations with teams, and record what has to change for AI to be used well.
- Write a change plan for AI adoption based on that assessment, with aims, activities and timescales.
- Name senior sponsors and set aside a budget and people for change work, separate from delivery.
- Make a change plan or a proportionate change section a requirement for every significant use of AI, checked at the stage gates (POR-04).

Pitfalls:

- Treating AI adoption as a tool rollout and putting all the budget into technology.
- Writing a plan without first finding out how people work and feel today.
- Naming sponsors who have no time or authority to act.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there a change plan for AI adoption, and who sponsors it?
- What people and budget are assigned to change, as opposed to delivery?
- How is the change approach applied to a new use of AI going live?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The AI change plan, with sponsors, resources and timescales
- Change plans or impact assessments for recent uses of AI

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No change approach; AI tools are made available and people are left to work out what to do with them.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some change activity happens on individual projects, but there is no organisation-wide plan or dedicated resource.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A documented AI change plan, based on an assessment of the current culture, has named senior sponsors and funded resource, and is applied to every significant use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progress against the change plan is measured and reported, and areas where adoption is stalling are identified and given extra support.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The change approach is refined from what has and has not worked in earlier rollouts and from changes in the scale and type of AI being adopted.

- AI change plan with sponsors and resources
- Change section template for individual uses of AI

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Staff receive clear, honest and regular communication about what AI is being used for, why, and what it means for them. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A communication plan for AI is in place and has an owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The plan sets out regular, honest messages about AI use, its purpose, its limits and its effect on staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The messages reach all staff.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
In the absence of information, people assume the worst, usually that AI is being brought in to cut jobs. Open communication, including about limits and problems, builds the trust that adoption depends on.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name an owner for internal communication about AI.
- Write a communication plan that sets the channels and frequency, and commits to covering what AI is used for, why, its limits and its effect on staff.
- Publish regular updates that include problems and limits as well as benefits, and keep a list of planned and live uses of AI that staff can see.
- Check that the plan reaches all staff, including those without regular computer access or on leave.

Pitfalls:

- Only announcing successes, which staff quickly stop believing.
- Avoiding the question of jobs, which leaves people to assume the worst.
- Leaving communication to suppliers or enthusiasts.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do staff find out which uses of AI are planned or live, and why?
- Does communication cover limits, problems and the effect on jobs, as well as benefits?
- How do you know the messages have been understood?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The communication plan and a sample of recent messages
- Staff survey or pulse results on understanding of AI use

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Communication about AI is occasional, comes from enthusiasts or suppliers, and is not coordinated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Announcements are made about some uses of AI, but they focus on benefits, are irregular or reach only some staff.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An owned communication plan delivers regular, honest messages to all staff about AI use, purpose, limits and effect on staff.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Reach and understanding are measured, for example through surveys, and messages are adjusted where staff are confused or concerned.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Communication is two-way as a matter of course, and its content and channels are improved from staff feedback and observed understanding.

- AI communication plan
- Staff-facing list of planned and live uses of AI
- Regular update template

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Staff and their representatives, including trade unions where present, are involved early in decisions about AI that affect their work, and their input is considered and answered. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined route is in place for engaging affected staff and their representatives on uses of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Affected staff and their representatives are involved at the design stage of each significant use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Their input is recorded.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: They are told what changed as a result of their input.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
The people who do the work know where AI will help and where it will cause problems. Involving them and their representatives before decisions are made produces better uses of AI and avoids the resistance that follows when change is presented as already decided.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define what counts as a significant use of AI that needs staff engagement, and add engagement to the design stage of the stage gates (POR-04).
- Agree with representative bodies, where they exist, how and when they will be involved.
- Hold engagement sessions with affected staff and representatives during design and record what they said.
- Report back to those involved what changed as a result of their input, and what did not and why.

Pitfalls:

- Consulting on a plan that has already been decided.
- Recording input but never telling people what happened to it.
- Engaging only with managers and not with the staff who do the work.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- At what point are affected staff involved in a proposed use of AI?
- Where representative bodies exist, how and when are they engaged?
- Can you show a case where staff input changed a decision about AI?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Engagement records or minutes from staff and representative meetings about AI
- Examples of designs or decisions changed after staff input

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Staff and representatives hear about AI after decisions are made, if at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Engagement happens on some projects or late in the process, often as consultation on a decided plan.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Affected staff and their representatives are involved at design stage of significant uses of AI through a defined route, their input is recorded, and they hear what changed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The timing and effect of engagement are tracked, and uses of AI that skipped it are identified and addressed.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Staff and representatives help shape the AI agenda itself, and the engagement approach is improved from their feedback on how well it works.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Engagement route description
- Engagement record template
- You said, we did summary

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Anyone can raise a concern or report a problem with AI without fear of blame, and can see what was done about it. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A no-blame route for raising AI concerns is in place and has an owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The route has been communicated to all staff.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People who raise a concern receive a response on what was done.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
The first signs that AI is producing wrong or harmful results are usually noticed by the people using it. If they fear blame or expect nothing to happen, they stay quiet and the problem grows.

Reaching Level 3:

- Choose or set up a route for raising AI concerns, which can be an existing route explicitly extended to cover AI, and name its owner.
- Write down that concerns raised in good faith will not lead to blame, and get senior leaders to say so publicly.
- Tell all staff about the route, with examples of the kinds of AI concerns it is for.
- Log each concern and give the person who raised it a response on what was done, with links to the incident process (MON-04) where needed.

Pitfalls:

- Assuming staff know that a general whistleblowing policy covers AI.
- Taking concerns in but never telling the person what happened.
- Making the route anonymous only, so there is no way to reply.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- If a member of staff thought an AI tool was giving wrong or unfair results, what would they do?
- How do you know staff feel safe to raise AI concerns?
- What happens after a concern is raised, and does the person hear back?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Guidance describing the route for raising AI concerns
- A log of concerns raised, with responses and outcomes
- Staff survey results on confidence in speaking up

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: There is no known route for raising AI concerns; problems are raised informally or not at all.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A route exists, such as a general helpdesk or whistleblowing policy, but staff do not know it covers AI or doubt that it is safe to use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: An owned, no-blame route for raising AI concerns is known to all staff, and everyone who raises a concern hears what was done.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Use of the route and staff confidence in it are measured, and response times and outcomes are monitored and reported.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Raising concerns is seen as normal practice, and the route and the response to it are improved from staff feedback and trends in what is raised.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Guidance on raising AI concerns
- Concerns log with responses
- No-blame statement from leadership

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Experiments and uses of AI that fail or are stopped are reviewed without blame, and the lessons are recorded and shared. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A no-blame review is held for every stopped or failed AI experiment or use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Lessons from each review are recorded in a shared place.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Lessons are communicated to the relevant teams.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Many AI experiments should not continue, and stopping them is a sign the process works. If stopped work is hidden or treated as failure, teams repeat the same mistakes and become unwilling to try things.

Reaching Level 3:

- Set a short no-blame review format, focused on what happened and what to do differently, not on who was at fault.
- Make the review a required step whenever an AI experiment or use is stopped or fails, linked to the stop decision (POR-07).
- Record lessons in one shared place that anyone proposing AI can search.
- Send each new lesson to the teams it is relevant to, for example through the community of practice (CUL-06).

Pitfalls:

- Reviewing only failures and not work that was stopped for good reasons.
- Writing long reports nobody reads instead of short, searchable lessons.
- Letting reviews turn into blame, which makes teams hide problems next time.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What happened to the last AI experiment that was stopped, and what was learned?
- Where are lessons recorded, and who reads them?
- How are teams who stop an experiment treated?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Review records for stopped or failed AI work
- A lessons log or library, with evidence it is used in new proposals

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Stopped or failed work is quietly dropped; lessons stay with the people involved.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some teams review what went wrong, but findings are not recorded or shared beyond the team.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every stopped or failed AI experiment or use has a no-blame review, and its lessons are recorded in a shared place and passed to relevant teams.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Lessons are checked for take-up, for example in new proposals and stage gates, and repeat mistakes are identified and followed up.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Lessons from inside and outside the organisation are used routinely to shape new proposals, and stopping work early is recognised as good practice.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- No-blame review template
- Shared lessons log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Networks of champions and communities of practice, with time and support to do so, spread know-how about AI and good practice across the organisation. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A champions network covers all major business areas.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Champions have a defined role and agreed time for it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A community of practice for AI meets regularly.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The community of practice receives central support.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
People learn most from colleagues doing similar work. A supported network of champions reaches parts of the organisation that central teams cannot, and brings practical problems back to the centre.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a champion role description that sets out what champions do and how much time they get, and agree that time with their managers.
- Recruit champions so that every major business area has at least one.
- Set up a community of practice that meets regularly, with a central contact who supports it and passes issues to the people who can act.
- Keep a list of champions by area and a record of community meetings.

Pitfalls:

- Asking champions to do the role on top of a full workload with no agreed time.
- Concentrating champions in technical teams and leaving front-line areas uncovered.
- Treating the network as a substitute for a resourced support route (PPL-08).

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Is there a network of AI champions, and which parts of the organisation does it cover?
- How much time do champions have for the role, and who supports them?
- How do issues raised by champions reach the people who can act on them?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Champion role description and a list of champions by area
- Community of practice meeting records or activity data

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: A few enthusiasts help colleagues on their own initiative and in their own time.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: A champions network or community exists in some areas, but without agreed time, support or a link to the central AI team.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A champions network with defined roles and agreed time covers all major business areas, and a centrally supported community of practice meets regularly.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Champion coverage and activity are tracked, and the network's effect on adoption and good practice is measured and reported.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The network shapes guidance, tools and priorities, and its structure is refreshed as adoption spreads and needs change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Champion role description
- Champions list by business area
- Community of practice meeting record

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Teams whose work changes because of AI get practical support through the change, and actual adoption is tracked against what was planned. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every team affected by a significant use of AI has a support plan.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each support plan covers process changes, time to adapt and help after go-live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Adoption is tracked against planned levels.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Going live is not the same as being used well. Teams need time, help and adjusted processes to change how they work, and without tracking nobody knows whether a tool is being used as intended, worked around or ignored.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a support plan template that covers process changes, time for teams to adapt and help after go-live.
- Require a completed support plan for every team affected by a significant use of AI before it goes live.
- Agree planned adoption levels for each rollout, such as how many people use the tool and for which tasks.
- Track actual adoption against those levels after go-live and share the results with the team and its business owner.

Pitfalls:

- Stopping support at launch week, when most adjustment happens later.
- Measuring logins rather than whether the tool is used for the intended work.
- Expecting teams to adapt without time set aside from their normal workload.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a recent use of AI, what support did the affected team receive before and after go-live?
- How do you know whether the team is actually using it as intended?
- What happens when adoption is lower than planned?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Support plans for teams affected by recent rollouts
- Adoption tracking data compared with planned levels

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Teams are given the tool and expected to adapt; nobody checks whether it is used.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some teams get support at launch, but it stops soon after and adoption is not tracked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every team affected by a significant use of AI has a support plan for the change, and adoption is tracked against planned levels.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Adoption data is reviewed regularly, teams falling behind receive targeted support, and the reasons for low adoption are recorded and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Support approaches are improved from adoption patterns across many rollouts, and new rollouts plan support from that evidence.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Team support plan template
- Adoption tracking sheet against planned levels

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation understands how the people it serves view its use of AI and takes that into account in its decisions and how it explains itself. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined approach is in place and used to gather the views of the people the organisation serves on its use of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: These views are considered in design decisions on uses of AI.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: These views are considered in how uses of AI are explained.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
An organisation's use of AI can be lawful and still lose the confidence of the people it serves. Knowing their views and expectations early lets it avoid uses they would not accept and explain the ones they would.

Reaching Level 3:

- Decide how you will gather the views of the people you serve on your AI use, such as surveys, panels, user research or reviews of complaints.
- Gather those views on a regular basis and for significant new uses of AI.
- Add a step in design reviews where those views are considered, and record the result.
- Use what you learn to shape how each use of AI is explained to the people it affects.

Pitfalls:

- Relying on complaints and media coverage as the only source of public views.
- Gathering views and not recording how they affected any decision.
- Asking only people who already support the use of AI.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What do you know about how the people you serve feel about your use of AI?
- How have their views affected a decision about using AI?
- How would you find out if trust in your use of AI was falling?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Research, surveys or panel findings on public or customer views of AI use
- Decision records showing those views were considered

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Public or customer views on the organisation's AI use are not sought; reaction is discovered only through complaints or media coverage.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Views are gathered occasionally, for example on a single project, but are not used consistently in decisions.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: The views of the people the organisation serves on its AI use are gathered through a defined approach and shape design decisions and explanations.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Levels of trust are measured over time, and changes in trust or emerging concerns lead to recorded action.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The people served help shape decisions about where and how AI is used, and the approach to building trust is improved from measured results.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Public and customer views approach
- Findings summary from research or surveys
- Design review record showing views considered

parts.name: overview
parts.prose: Covers what happens once AI is in use: setting measures before go-live, monitoring live behaviour, tracking whether benefits arrive, handling non-security incidents and notifying serious ones, independent assurance, listening to users, re-running this assessment and reporting to leadership. Without measurement the organisation cannot tell whether AI is working, causing harm or worth its cost.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Each use of AI has agreed performance measures and a recorded baseline of current performance before it goes live. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every use of AI has agreed measures covering accuracy, service outcome and effect on people, with a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A baseline for each measure is recorded before go-live.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Measures include reliance, meaning how often outputs are accepted, checked or overridden, compared with measured accuracy so that overreliance and underreliance show up.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Risks that cannot yet be measured are recorded, with the indicators or proxies used to track them.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Where the environmental footprint of a use is material, measures include it, such as energy, compute and water, with a baseline.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Without a baseline taken before go-live, nobody can show later whether AI made things better or worse. Agreeing measures in advance also stops success being defined after the event to fit whatever happened.

Reaching Level 3:

- For each use of AI, agree measures with a named owner covering accuracy, service outcome and effect on people, plus environmental footprint where it is material.
- Include a reliance measure, such as how often outputs are accepted, checked or overridden, and plan to compare it with measured accuracy.
- Record a baseline for every measure before go-live, using current performance of the process the AI will support.
- List any risks that cannot yet be measured and set the indicators or proxies you will use to track them.

Pitfalls:

- Measuring only technical accuracy and missing the effect on people and services.
- Setting measures after go-live, when no baseline can be taken.
- Ignoring reliance, so people accepting wrong outputs without checking goes unseen.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a recent use of AI, what measures were agreed and when?
- What was the baseline before go-live, and how was it measured?
- Do the measures cover effects on people as well as technical performance?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Measure definitions and baseline data for a sample of uses of AI
- Stage gate records showing measures were checked
- Recorded risks that cannot yet be measured, with their proxy indicators
- Reliance measures compared with accuracy for live uses

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Measures are not set; success is judged by impression or anecdote.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some uses of AI have measures, but they are set after go-live, lack a baseline or cover only technical performance.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every use of AI has owned measures of accuracy, outcome, effect on people and reliance, with baselines set before go-live and proxies for risks not yet measurable.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Measures and baselines are checked at stage gates, and uses without them are stopped or held until they are in place.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Measures are refined from experience of which ones actually predicted success or problems, and common measures allow comparison across uses.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Measures and baseline template for each use
- Unmeasurable risks and proxies list

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Live AI is monitored against its measures for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour, with thresholds that trigger action. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every live use of AI is monitored for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour against defined thresholds.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Event logging is enabled for each use of AI while it is in use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Named people are responsible for responding when thresholds are crossed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: AI provided by others is monitored against the provider's instructions for use.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use is monitored against its defined operating conditions.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use is monitored against the fairness measures set under RSK-06.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use is monitored for personal or sensitive data appearing in its outputs.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every action an agent takes in another system is logged with what triggered it, and a named person can stop each agent at once.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI that worked at go-live can degrade as data, users or the underlying model change, often without any visible failure. Continuous monitoring with set thresholds catches this before it causes harm.

Reaching Level 3:

- For each live use of AI, set thresholds for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour, using the measures from MON-01, the operating conditions and the fairness measures from RSK-06.
- Turn on event logging for each live use and add checks for personal or sensitive data appearing in outputs.
- For AI provided by others, add monitoring against the provider's instructions for use.
- Name the people who respond when a threshold is crossed and write down what they do.

Pitfalls:

- Monitoring availability and cost only, with no check on the quality of outputs.
- Setting thresholds with no named person to act when they are crossed.
- Assuming a supplier monitors its AI on your behalf.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How do you know a live use of AI is still performing as it did at go-live?
- What thresholds trigger action, and who acts?
- How would you detect AI being used for purposes it was not approved for?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Agent action logs, and a tested way to stop each agent
- Monitoring dashboards or reports for live uses of AI
- Records of threshold breaches and the action taken
- Event logs for live uses of AI, with their retention period
- Monitoring against operating conditions
- Live fairness and sensitive data monitoring results

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Live AI is not monitored; problems are found when users complain.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some uses are monitored, usually for availability or cost, without checks on output quality or thresholds for action.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every live use of AI is logged and monitored against thresholds, operating conditions, fairness measures and provider instructions, with named people to respond to breaches.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Monitoring results are reviewed on a set cycle, threshold breaches are tracked to resolution, and monitoring coverage is itself checked.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Whether the expected benefits of AI arrive is tracked and reported, for each use and across the portfolio, and shortfalls are acted on. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Benefits for each use of AI are tracked against its business case on a set schedule.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each use has a named owner for tracking its benefits.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Benefits are reported across the portfolio.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Benefits stated in a business case are forecasts, and many do not arrive in full or arrive later than planned. Tracking them shows which uses are worth continuing and keeps future business cases realistic.

Reaching Level 3:

- Take the expected benefits from each business case (POR-05) and record them with measures and dates.
- Name an owner for benefits on each use and set a schedule for checking them.
- Track actual benefits against the business case on that schedule.
- Combine the results into a portfolio report that shows each use and the total.

Pitfalls:

- Checking benefits once soon after launch and never again.
- Counting time saved without asking what that time is now used for.
- Leaving benefits ownership with the delivery team, which moves on after go-live.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- For a use of AI that has been live for some time, what benefits have actually been realised?
- Who tracks benefits, and how often?
- What happens when benefits fall short of the business case?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Benefits tracking records for a sample of uses of AI
- Portfolio benefits report comparing forecast and actual results

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Benefits are not tracked after approval.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Benefits are reviewed for some uses, usually once and informally, and not totalled across the portfolio.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A named owner tracks each use's benefits against its business case on a set schedule, and results are reported across the portfolio.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Benefit claims are checked against evidence, shortfalls trigger review of the use, and actual results are compared with forecasts.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Actual benefit data is used to calibrate new business cases and the organisation-level value case, and the tracking method is refined from experience.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Benefits register for each use
- Portfolio benefits report template

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: AI incidents and near misses that are not security incidents, such as wrong outputs, harm to people or misuse, are reported, investigated and learned from. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined process covers reporting, triage, investigation and resolution of non-security AI incidents and near misses.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A definition of an AI incident and a near miss is in place and staff understand it.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The process has a defined link to security incident handling.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: People affected by an AI incident that is not serious are told what happened and what is being done, in a way that suits the incident.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
AI fails in ways that ordinary incident processes often do not recognise, such as confident but wrong answers or unfair treatment of some groups. Recording near misses as well as incidents shows patterns early, while the cost is still low.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write a plain definition of a non-security AI incident and near miss, with examples, and a process for reporting, triage, investigation and resolution that hands security cases to SEC-05.
- Investigate each incident and near miss to its cause, record the resolution, and pass serious incidents to MON-09 for notification and any suspension.
- Tell staff how to report, using the route for raising concerns (CUL-04), and keep a log of incidents and near misses.

Pitfalls:

- Recording only incidents that caused harm and ignoring near misses.
- Leaving AI incidents in the general IT queue, where wrong or unfair outputs are not recognised.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What counts as an AI incident here, and how would staff report one?
- Are near misses recorded as well as incidents?
- Can you show an AI incident that led to a change?
- When an incident that is not serious affects people, how are they told?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The AI incident process and definition
- The incident and near miss log, with investigations and actions
- Examples of how affected people were told about lesser incidents

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: AI incidents are handled as they arise, if they are recognised at all; nothing is recorded.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some AI incidents are logged in general systems, but there is no agreed definition, investigation method or record of near misses.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A defined process, linked to security incident handling, covers reporting, triage, investigation and resolution of non-security AI incidents and near misses that staff can recognise.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Incident and near miss trends are analysed and reported, and actions are tracked to completion.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Lessons from incidents, including those reported by other organisations, routinely change designs, controls and training.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- AI incident definition and process
- Incident and near miss log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Uses of AI are reviewed by people independent of their delivery, with the depth and frequency of review proportionate to risk. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A defined assurance approach sets the depth and frequency of independent review for each risk tier.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Independent reviews are carried out on all uses of AI in line with the approach.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Reviews are also triggered by material change or emerging risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Reviews check compliance against the obligations register (RSK-04).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every finding is recorded, with an owner and a remediation date set by risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Findings are tracked, and their status is reported to leadership (MON-08).

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The AI governance arrangements as a whole are independently audited on a set cycle.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Teams that build or run a use of AI are not well placed to judge it objectively. Independent review gives leaders confidence that controls work in practice, and directs review effort to the uses that carry most risk.

Reaching Level 3:

- Write an assurance approach that sets the depth and frequency of independent review for each risk tier (RSK-02), covering all uses of AI in the inventory (GOV-06).
- Add triggers for extra reviews on material change or emerging risk, and include a check of compliance against the obligations register (RSK-04) in every review.
- Record each finding with an owner and a remediation date set by risk, and report status to leadership (MON-08).
- Arrange an independent audit of the AI governance arrangements as a whole on a set cycle, such as through internal audit or an external reviewer.

Pitfalls:

- Using reviewers from the delivery team's own line, who are not truly independent.
- Reviewing only high-profile uses and leaving lower-risk uses with no review at all.
- Recording findings without owners or dates, so they never close.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- Which uses of AI have had an independent review, and how was the reviewer independent?
- How is the depth and frequency of review decided?
- What happened to the findings of the last review?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Finding log with owners, remediation dates and status, and the record of the periodic audit of AI governance as a whole
- The assurance plan or schedule by risk tier
- Recent review reports with findings and action tracking

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: No independent review; delivery teams assure their own work.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Independent reviews happen for occasional high-profile uses, without a defined basis for which uses are reviewed or how.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every use of AI gets independent review set by risk tier and triggered by change, findings are owned and reported, and AI governance as a whole is audited periodically.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Assurance coverage against the plan is reported, findings are tracked to closure, and overdue actions are escalated.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: The assurance approach is refined from findings, incidents and external developments, and uses methods that test real behaviour as well as documents.

- Findings log with owners and dates
- Governance audit schedule

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Feedback from people who use AI and people affected by it is gathered on a regular basis, analysed, and acted on. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Every live use of AI has a way for users and affected people to give feedback.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A named owner reviews the feedback for each use on a set cycle.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The action taken on feedback is recorded.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Users and affected people see problems that measures miss, such as outputs that are technically correct but unhelpful or confusing. Acting visibly on their feedback also improves trust and take-up.

Reaching Level 3:

- Give every live use of AI a simple feedback route for users and affected people, such as a form, a button or a contact point.
- Name an owner for feedback on each use and set how often they review it.
- Record each review and the action taken, including where no action was needed and why.

Pitfalls:

- Collecting feedback only from staff users and not from the people affected by outputs.
- Collecting feedback at launch and then stopping.
- Treating feedback as a route to challenge a decision, which belongs under RSK-08.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How can users and affected people give feedback on a use of AI?
- Who reviews feedback, and how often?
- Can you show a change made because of feedback?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Feedback channels and a sample of feedback received
- Records of feedback reviews and resulting changes

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Feedback is not sought; what arrives comes through general complaints.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Feedback is gathered for some uses, usually at launch, but is not analysed or acted on consistently.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Every live use of AI has a feedback route for users and affected people, with a named owner who reviews it on a set cycle and records action.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Feedback trends are measured and reported alongside performance data, and recurring issues lead to tracked changes.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Feedback is built into the service, and the way it is gathered and used is improved from evidence of what leads to useful change.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Feedback route for each use
- Feedback review and action log

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation re-runs this framework's assessment on a set cycle, compares results with earlier ones, and acts on the gaps it finds. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The assessment is re-run on a set cycle by a named owner.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Each round's results are compared with the previous round.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: An improvement plan with owners is agreed after each round.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
A single assessment gives a snapshot that soon becomes out of date as AI use and the organisation change. Repeating it on a cycle shows whether improvement actions worked and where to focus next.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name an owner for the assessment and set a cycle for re-running it, such as yearly.
- Keep the results of each round in a form that can be compared with the next.
- Compare each new round with the previous one and record what moved and what did not.
- Agree an improvement plan with named owners for each action and get it approved by the executive sponsor.

Pitfalls:

- Running the assessment once and treating the result as permanent.
- Producing results with no improvement plan behind them.
- Changing the assessment method between rounds so results cannot be compared.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- When was the assessment last run, and when is the next one due?
- How do current results compare with the previous round?
- What improvement actions came out of the last assessment, and are they complete?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Completed assessments from at least two rounds
- The improvement plan with owners and progress

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: The assessment has been done once or not at all, and results were not acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: The assessment is repeated irregularly, or results are produced but not turned into an improvement plan.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: A named owner re-runs the assessment on a set cycle, compares results with the previous round, and agrees an improvement plan with owners.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Progress against the improvement plan is tracked and reported, and assessment results are checked against evidence rather than self-reported alone.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Target levels and the assessment cycle are adjusted from results and external change, and results are used to set priorities across the organisation.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Assessment schedule
- Round-by-round comparison sheet
- Improvement plan with owners

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Leadership and the board receive consolidated, evidence-based reporting on AI use, performance, benefits, incidents and risk, on a set cycle. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A consolidated report with an owner covers AI use, performance, benefits, incidents and risk.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The report is produced on a set cycle from defined data.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The report goes to leadership and the board.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Where the organisation answers to a parent body, regulator or group board, it gives a periodic signed assurance statement backed by auditable evidence.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
Leaders cannot oversee what they cannot see. Bringing measures, benefits, incidents and assurance findings into one report lets them judge the overall position and make decisions on evidence rather than anecdote.

Reaching Level 3:

- Name an owner for leadership reporting on AI and agree the reporting cycle with the board.
- Define the data for each section of the report: AI use from the inventory (GOV-06), performance from monitoring (MON-02), benefits (MON-03), incidents (MON-04) and risk.
- Produce one consolidated report on that cycle and send it to leadership and the board.
- Where you answer to a parent body, regulator or group board, add a signed assurance statement on the agreed cycle and keep the evidence behind it ready for audit.

Pitfalls:

- Sending a narrative update with no data behind it.
- Reporting each project separately, so leaders never see the whole picture.
- Signing assurance statements without keeping the evidence that supports them.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- What does leadership receive about AI, and how often?
- Where does the data in the report come from, and how is it checked?
- Can you show a leadership decision made on the basis of the report?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- Recent leadership or board reports on AI
- Minutes recording discussion and actions arising
- Signed assurance statements with their evidence, where required

parts.name: level

parts.prose: Leadership hears about AI through occasional updates or individual project reports.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some reporting reaches leadership, but it is not consolidated, is mostly narrative or covers only some uses of AI.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Leadership and the board receive an owned, consolidated AI report from defined data on a set cycle, with a signed assurance statement where the organisation answers upward.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: The data behind the report is checked for accuracy, leadership actions are tracked, and reporting shows trends against targets.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Report content is refined from what leaders use in decisions, and the report brings in external comparison and forward-looking indicators.

- Data source list for each report section
- Signed assurance statement with evidence pack

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The organisation defines serious AI incidents, can suspend a use of AI when needed, and tells suppliers, regulators and affected people through set routes and within set deadlines. At Level 3, every applicable criterion is met.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Serious AI incidents are defined.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: The definition of serious incidents meets what applicable law requires.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Routes and deadlines for notifying suppliers of a serious incident are set.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: Routes and deadlines for notifying regulators of a serious incident are set.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A decision point to suspend a use of AI after a serious incident is defined.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: A plan is in place for telling affected people about a serious incident.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: When a use of AI presents a risk to health, safety or rights short of a serious incident, the supplier is told and use is suspended if needed.

parts.name: item
parts.prose: When the law requires it, the regulator is also told of such a risk.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
When AI causes or risks serious harm, the law may set short deadlines for telling the supplier and the regulator, and the people affected need to hear promptly. Deciding in advance what counts as serious, who can suspend a use and who must be told means these duties are met under pressure rather than missed.

Reaching Level 3:

- Define serious AI incidents as applicable law requires, using the obligations register (RSK-04).
- Set routes and deadlines for notifying suppliers and regulators of a serious incident, and a plan for telling affected people.
- Set a decision point and a named decision maker to suspend a use of AI after a serious incident.
- Where a use presents a risk to health, safety or rights short of a serious incident, tell the supplier, and the regulator where the law requires, and suspend the use if needed.
- Link these steps to the incident process (MON-04) so serious cases are recognised and escalated at triage.

Pitfalls:

- Not deciding in advance who can suspend a use of AI, so suspension is delayed.
- Waiting for an investigation to finish before notifying, and missing a legal deadline.

parts.name: assessment-questions
parts.prose:
- How are serious AI incidents defined here, and does the definition follow what the law requires?
- Who can suspend a use of AI after a serious incident, and how quickly can they act?
- Who must be told of a serious incident or a risk to health, safety or rights, by when, and how would affected people be told?

parts.name: expected-evidence
parts.prose:
- The serious incident definition and the legal source it follows
- Notification routes and deadlines for suppliers and regulators
- Suspension decision records, with the named decision maker
- The plan for telling affected people about a serious incident

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 1: Initial
parts.prose: Serious AI incidents are handled case by case; nobody has decided who must be told or who can suspend a use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 2: Developing
parts.prose: Some notification duties are known, but serious incidents are not defined, deadlines are not set, or no one is named to suspend a use.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 3: Defined
parts.prose: Serious AI incidents are defined, notification routes and deadlines and a decision point to suspend use are set, affected people are told under a plan, and risks short of a serious incident are reported and acted on.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 4: Managed
parts.prose: Serious incidents lead to reviews of the use concerned, and notification and suspension decisions are reviewed with their actions tracked to completion.

parts.name: level
parts.title: Level 5: Optimising
parts.prose: Lessons from serious incidents, including those reported by other organisations, routinely change designs, controls and notification arrangements.

parts.name: artefacts
parts.prose:
- Notification routes and deadlines table
- Suspension decision record
- Plan for telling affected people
